NOTES John Frederick Lewis showed his first Royal Academy exhibit in 1821, well before he was 20 but he did not become a full Royal Academician until he was over 60. Unlike his friend Edwin Landseer, his career did not follow a straight course, as, in the meantime he was for over 30 years a member of the Old Water-Colour Society, being elected its President in 1855, only to resign less than three years later in order to devote more energy to the more lucrative medium of oil painting. The son of a successful engraver, Frederick Christian Lewis, whose trade he learnt, he gained early success as a painter of animals and sporting subjects, but, after a trip to Europe in 1826/27, he became more interested in the people and architecture of foreign places, finding watercolour a natural medium. A visit to Spain in 1832-34 reinforced these inclinations, and the watercolours and lithographs that resulted were widely acclaimed. Such success encouraged him to seek more exotic subjects further afield and from Italy in 1840 he journeyed via Alabania and Greece to Constantinople. After a year, he continued on to Egypt. Lewis then spent a decade, 1841-51, living and working in Cairo, at a time when few British artists had visited the city and even fewer had devoted attention to the everyday life of the people that inhabited it. Among the subjects especially favoured by Lewis were the streets and covered markets in the centre of the city, surrounding the impressive architecture of its Mamluk mosques and mausolea. He made a number of detailed but - perhaps deliberately - apparently unfinished pencil and watercolour sketches of these streets and bazaars, capturing the light and atmosphere of the vast spaces and accurately depicting the complex architectural features of the buildings with their intricately carved and banded stonework, wooden structures and textile awnings. These drawings were seen by Lewis's friend, the writer William Makepeace Thackeray, when he visited Cairo in 1844, towards the end of his tour around the eastern Mediterranean and they are mentioned in his later account of the trip, Notes of a Journey from Cornhill to Grand Cairo (1846). Describing his own astonishment at the scenes in Cairo that confronted him, he wrote: 'How to describe the beauty of the streets to you! - the fantastic splendour; the variety of the houses, and archways, and hanging roofs, and balconies, and porches; the delightful accidents of light and shade which chequer them; the noise, the bustle, the brilliancy of the crowd; the interminable vast bazaars with their barbaric splendour! There is a fortune to be made for painters in Cairo, and materials for a whole Academy of them. I never saw such a variety of architecture, of life, of picturesqueness, of brilliant colour, and light and shade. There is a picture in every street, and at every bazaar stall. Some of these, our celebrated water-colour painter, Mr Lewis, has produced with admirable truth and exceeding minuteness and beauty; but there is room for a hundred to follow him...'. A brilliant essayist and novelist, Thackeray's account of his journey combines fact and fiction in a typically idiosyncratic way. The description of his visit to Lewis that follows shortly after this passage is littered with double entendres aimed at a western audience already sated with a large body of popular travel literature. While Thackeray may deliberately have sensationalised his account of Lewis, much in it can be corroborated by the fragments of information that exist in letters from other European visitors and, read carefully, Thackeray's text reveals a great deal both about Lewis's life in Cairo and about the image of it that writer and artist wished to convey. Lewis, wrote Thackeray 'has established himself here in the most complete Oriental fashion' in a house, 'far away from the haunts of European civilisation, in the Arab quarter... situated in a cool, shady, narrow alley'. On entering the 'broad open court' he encountered 'the walls of his long, queer, many-windowed, many-galleried house' and was ushered into a 'hall of audience' with a ceiling 'carved, gilt, painted and embroidered with arabesques and choice sentences of Eastern writing'. At last 'J' appeared, but utterly changed from the sartorial frequenter of clubs he had known in London and Paris: 'A man - in a long yellow gown, with a long beard, somewhat tinged with grey, with his head shaved, and wearing on it first a white wadded cotton night-cap, second, a red tarboosh...' After a time however 'his oriental coolness and languor gave way to British cordiality' and he became again the amusing companion of former days. 'He has adapted himself outwardly, however, to the oriental life. When he goes abroad he rides a grey horse with red housings, and has two servants to walk beside him. He wears a very handsome grave costume of dark blue, consisting of an embroidered jacket and gaiters, and a pair of trousers, which would make a set of dresses for an English family. His beard curls nobly over his chest, his Damascus scimitar on his thigh. His red cap gives him a venerable and Bey-like appearance'. Thus attired, Lewis was well placed to roam the streets of Cairo and while his 'disguise' is unlikely to have fooled anybody it would at least have enabled him to observe the activities of the city's inhabitants at close quarters. Lewis lived a dual existence: he adopted the dress and customs of Cairo's Turkish elite, but retained many British habits, eating meat, as Thackeray noted, 'with an Infidel knife and fork' and drinking 'certain sherberts, prepared by the two great rivals, Hadji Hodson and Bass Bey'. He associated with the expatriate community, being described by Henry Abbott, another long-standing member of this group, as 'an excellent fellow, liked by everyone', he ordered tea from a British merchant in Alexandria and collected antiquities as well as the items of Egyptian costume, oriental procelain and artefacts that he later used extensively as props in his paintings. While conveying an impression of indolence - Thackery's 'languid Lotus-eater' - he was actively working to accumulate a large number of sketches and a few full-size compositions. While immersed in an Islamic society, he was at the same time engaged in the particularly European activity of recording and interpreting an 'alien' people for a 'home' audience. In 1851 Lewis returned to England, following the enormous acclaim with which his watercolour, The Hhareem, was received the previous year when it was exhibited at the Old Water-Colour Society. Armed with his store of sketches and his collection of costume and artefacts, he continued, over the next twenty-five years, to exhibit scenes of oriental life - bedouin with their camels in the desert, women gorgeously attired in interiors suffused with dappled light or in lush gardens surrounded by flowers, and traders, entertainers, scribes and other inhabitants of the bazaars and coffee-houses of Cairo. The present example is undated and is not known to have been exhibited, although it may be identifiable or be connected with either of two paintings that Lewis exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1862, A street in Cairo (no. 797) and Bazaar, Cairo (no. 815). In subject it relates closely to an oil painting exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1869, The seraff (money-changer), a doubtful coin; a scene in a Cairo bazaar (Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery). As in the latter painting, the man on the left, seated on a mastaba, turbanned and with a dark instead of a grey beard, holds up what appears to be a coin for examination, brought to him by the two veiled women in front of him. To their right stands the merchant with his lengths of cloth and his young black assistant waiting for the verdict on the disputed authenticity of the coin. Currency was a problem in Egypt in the late 1840s, as Lord Castlereagh, who was there in 1842, relates. Both Turkish and Egyptian money was in circulation, but since the hostilities between the Sultan of Turkey and the Pasha of Egypt, Muhammed Ali, Turkish currency was no longer legal tender. 'The consequence is', wrote Castlereagh, 'that every one who pays, endeavours to pass away some Turkish money, and in the old currency it is extremely difficult for a foreigner to tell the difference. Then again, many of the Pasha's pieces of gold have been depreciated, and clipped or split. These the people object to take at their value, and deduct half or a whole piastre, as they think expedient'. (Viscount Castlereagh, Journey to Damascus through Egypt, Nubia, Arabia Petrae, Palestine, and Syria, 1847, Vol. I, pp. 39-40). According to E.W. Lane, the great 19th century Arabist and author of An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836) 'seyrefees' or money-changers were often Jews and were held in high esteem for their integrity. Hence the disputants reliance on him for a fair judgement. The grouping of two women before an older, respected man, and the similar group which occupies the central space in the 1869 Doubtful Coin, may be derived from a similar arrangement of figures in David Wilkie's The Turkish Letter-Writer (Aberdeen Art Gallery and Museums), painted in 1840 while the artist was in Constantinople. Lewis, who knew and had a huge admiration for the older artist, was there at the same time. The two men communicated several times and on occasions sketched the same subjects, so it would not be surprising if one of the watercolours that Lewis exhibited soon after his return to England, The Arab Scribe - Cairo (1852; Private Collection), in which a similar group holds centre stage, was intended as a tribute to Wilkie, who had died at sea on the way home from the East, or that Lewis should re-employ with variations so successful a formula in later compositions. In A Doubtful Coin the narrative forms the central focus for the composition; whereas in the present painting it is part of a larger scene depicting the crowded thoroughfare of one of Cairo's busiest street markets. Indeed it seems to have been introduced at a fairly late stage since it is not present in the same format in the watercolour study for the painting (Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery). To acquire credibility as a painter of eastern scenes Lewis relied on an accumulation of realistic detail - architecture, costume, objects, gestures - and placed his protagonists in identifiable settings. The Ghuriyya would have been known to Lewis's public through one of the images in David Roberts's popular series of lithographs, Egypt and Nubia (1849, Vol III, Pl. 96, Bazaar of the Silk-Mercers, Cairo ), and would have been recognisable from the red and white banded walls and elaborate doorways and windows of the early 16th century mosque complex of Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri, the mausoleum (with the sabil and kuttab ) on the left and mosque- madrasa on the right facing each other across the street. The trader with his colourful silks and cottons and the bolts of fabric stacked up in the stalls against the buildings indicate the type of merchandise sold in the area. In order to achieve his goal of presenting an 'authentic' event in recognisable surroundings, the artist adds colour, movement and narrative detail to the architectural setting. Inevitably the fluidity and fine pencil work that makes the on-the-spot drawing (Witt Collection, Courtauld Institute of Art) so remarkable is sacrificed. A similar transformation takes place between the vertical format drawing of the Ghuriyya from the opposite direction (Opp‚ Collection, Tate, London) and the finished watercolour (signed and dated 1876; Sotheby's, 13 November 1997, lot 139) painted in the studio of his Surrey house approximately thirty years later. Nevertheless when its almost identical oil counterpart was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1877, the year after Lewis's death, with the title The street and mosque of the Ghoreeyah, Cairo, it was applauded in the Art Journal as 'showing all that exquisite detail, brilliant colouring and deft play of light for which his pictures were always so conspicuous' (1877, p. 269). (This painting was exhibited at the Fine Art Society, Recent Acquisitions, 1969, no. 71, went to an American private collection but was subsequently accidentally destroyed.) Also evident in the current painting, these are the qualities for which Lewis had been feted throughout his life. One of his staunchest champions was the influential art critic John Ruskin who hailed him in Praeterita as 'the painter of greatest power, next to Turner, in the English School'. Shorly before he died Lewis received a glowing tribute from his fellow artist, Edward Lear: 'There never have been & there never will be, any works depicting oriental life - more truly beautiful and excellent..... For besides the exquisite and conscientious workmanship, the subjects painted by J.F. Lewis were perfect as representations of real scenes and people' (letter to Lewis's wife Marian, 22 June 1875, Private Collection). A more critical 21st-century appraisal of Lewis's paintings might emphasise their presentation of a stereotypical view of Near Eastern life, but it should also appreciate the factual base in which each element of the composition is rooted and the absence of the moral undertones that inform so many other Victorian portrayals of Islamic society. portrayals of Islamic society.

The first generation, such as Delacroix, Vernet, Colin and Chass‚riau were inspired by political events such as Napoleon's conquest of Algeria and the liberation of Greece. Artists from the second half of the century such as G‚r“me, Bauernfeind, Deutsch and Ernst were more interested in depicting scenes from daily life. Ernst's first taste of the East was sparked by journeys to Moorish Spain, Morocco and Tunis in the second half of the 1880s, followed by a visit to Constantinople and Egypt in 1890. Ernst was especially impressed by Islamic ceramics and tiles and those in his collection reappear in many of his works. Ernst left Paris in 1905 to live in Fontenay-aux-Roses, where he decorated his home in an Ottoman style and lived among the objects which figured so largely in his paintings. Heavily influenced by the academic style of Jean-L‚on G‚r“me, both Ludwig Deutsch and Rudolf Ernst implemented the French master's exactitude in detail and intensity of colour. NOTES Hailed as the greatest Orientalist painter the English School has ever produced, John Frederick Lewis left a surviving oeuvre of no less than two thousand sketches, watercolors, drawings and paintings. Born into an artistic family in 1805, the son of an engraver, Lewis was strongly urged by his father to join the family business. He envisioned himself as a painter and draughtsman however and his remarkable talent, evident at a young age, led him to exhibit at the Royal Academy in 1821 at the age of sixteen. He also earned membership to the prestigious Old Watercolor Society in 1827. After working in England and exhibiting around the country, it was not long before Lewis yearned to travel abroad. An early two-year sojourn in southern Spain and Morocco in 1832 would prove crucial to his future development as an Orientalist for it was here that he first encountered the intriguing new subject matter that would occupy him for the rest of his career. Enchanted by the sun-drenched Islamic mosques and the unique Moorish architecture of the Alhambra Palace, with its decorative courtyards, elegant archways and fountains, Lewis, fired up with enthusiasm, expanded his travels to Turkey and North Africa in pursuit of the "exotic". Yet unlike his other artistic contemporaries who made the traditional Orientalist pilgrimage, Lewis would spend nearly a decade in Egypt. The years spanning 1840-51 found the artist firmly entrenched in Arab life. Adopting the Arab dress and customs, his lengthy residence in Cairo as "a kind of aristocratic vagabond in the East" inspired some of his greatest compositions - a rich and varied repertory of works featuring harem beauties, rugged desert encampments and crowded Cairo streets and markets. The Bezestein Bazaar of El Khan Khalil, Cairo, is undoubtedly, the Orientalist tour de force of Lewis's late oeuvre. Painted in 1872 in his studio in Walton-on-Thames, it is one of his largest oils and represents the artist at the pinnacle of his creative powers. This celebrated composition - a stunning visual spectacle of a traditional Egyptian suk or marketplace - stands as a sort of artistic memoir of a life-long passion for Egypt, based on numerous sketches of people and places he encountered. Widely exhibited, the work drew positive reviews - the canvas's larger format representing a departure from the artist's usual smaller scale works. One reviewer wrote, "We have been so long accustomed to discourse with Mr. Lewis over his small pieces of microscopic finish, that anything larger brings with it a surprise for which there has been no preparation". He further praised the work as "a very spirited composition every passage of which is undoubtedly true". ( Art Journal, 1872, p. 282). But even before the R.A. show, his friend and fellow artist, Thomas Woolner would write, "You do not think so highly of your work as your admirers do, or you could not be surprised at any sum being offered for one of your chief pictures...very soon your works will be priceless" (Woolner to Lewis, 17 May 1874, Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection). Soon after the opening it is recorded that a collector from Glasgow made a private offer to buy the present work for the then generous sum of 10,000 gns. - an offer however stridently refused by the painting's first owner, David Price. It was Lewis's full immersion in Cairo life that not only enriched his understanding of the complex city but provided the impetus for his sensitive artistic portrayals. Dressed in native garb and at ease with the language, he easily disappeared into the crowd to observe and sketch for hours, later building up his oil compositions in his studio. Lewis was further compelled to live in the Ezbekiya quarter of Cairo, a residential area in the north of the city - "the most Ottoman quarter of Cairo" - far from the British ex-patriot community. There are many detailed accounts by friends who had a chance to observe the artist's lifestyle as an oriental pasha (fig. 1). After a visit to Lewis's residence, friend William Thackeray provides one of the most colorful descriptions: First we came into a broad open court, with a covered gallery running along one side of it. A camel was reclining on the grass there; near him was a gazelle...and a numerous brood of hens and chickens, who furnish his liberal table. On the opposite side of the covered gallery rose up the walls of his long queer many-windowed, many-galleried house...while I was examining the strange apartments and all its contents, my respect and awe for the owner increased vastly. So profound was Lewis's transformation into an oriental pasha that Thackeray failed to recognize his friend. Lewis entered dressed "in a long yellow gown, with a long beard, somewhat tinged with grey, with his head shaved, and wearing on it first a white wadded cotton nightcap, second, a red tarboosh. It was some time, as the Americans say, before I could 'realise' the semillant J. of old times" (Thackeray, Notes of a Journey from Cornhill to Cairo, 1846, pp. 377-81). The district of Khan el-Khalili, home to a vast network of markets, was one of the most important trading centers in Cairo. Also known as the Turkish bazaar during the Ottoman period, the complex dates back to the fourteenth century when it was built by the Emir Djaharks el-Khalili in the heart of the Fatimid city in medieval Cairo. Bazaar culture has always been a central component of Arab life throughout the centuries, important not only to the commercial livelihood of the country but as a focal point for community gatherings. In larger cities, markets were defined by their quarter and were clustered around a mosque and hamman or public bath. During Lewis's residence, in the mid-19th Century, Egypt under the Mamluk dynasty flourished as a trading center. From the documentary architectural evidence afforded by present work, Caroline H. Williams has recently confirmed that the market Lewis has depicted here is in fact the great Ghuriyya market, the main cloth market of Cairo and a southern extension of El Khan Khalili. Named after the ruling 16th Century Sultan Al-Ghuri, the complex is anchored by two buildings that sit opposite each other on the main ceremonial street of medieval Cairo - the Mosque-Madrasa to the east and the Mausoleum-Sabil-Kuttab to the west. These bustling streets ranked as favorite areas among Western artists such as David Roberts and Owen B. Carter who were among the first to depict the Ghuriyya. In 1851 Lewis's Street and Mosque of the Gouriah (Lewis, no. 516) shows a view of the more open markets running along the street. The present work is unique in that Lewis has chosen to depict the less touristed covered Ghuriyya market located to the west of the Mosque Madrasa building. Confronted by the exhausting maze of the grand market, Lewis successfully captures the energy of a bustling Arab bazaar. In contrast to his earlier market scenes that emphasized smaller compositional groups or individual portrayals of merchants, ( In the Bezestein Bazaar, Cairo, 1860; (Lewis, 1978, no. 582) and A Cairo Bazaar; The Dellal ; Lewis, 1978, no. 618), the present composition is his grandest and most animated depiction of the interior of a bazaar. A long narrow structure with vaulted ceilings, the market is defined by rows of stalls where merchants display their fine silks and fabrics. While much of the day was spent hawking goods to clients, there was ample time for socializing. In the foreground of the composition Lewis has set up a dialogue between the two groups of wealthy merchants who, during a musical interlude, engage in smoking, eating and idle conversation. Stylistically, the present work represents the successful fusion of Lewis's skillful draughtsmanship with his ongoing experimentation with color and atmospheric effects. Although Lewis drew considerable praise for his virtuoso handling of the watercolor medium, he was equally skilled with oils and in the 1850s it became his preferred media, not to mention more commerically valuable. Whatever the medium, Lewis strove for a highly polished surface. As shown in the present work, the brushwork denotes a precision and delicacy and, when coupled with the robust red, blue, and green hues that contrast against the darkened interior, the overall effect is mesmerizing. Lewis crowds the majority of the merchants into the foreground, yet does not subordinate detail to the quantity of figures. From the intricately patterned fabrics to other decorative embellishments such as the hookah and the bowl of freshly cut fruit, Lewis lavishes his attentions on the exquisite dress and shop trinkets. The degree of detail achieved is not surprising due to his immense personal collection of objects, instruments and clothing which he brought back to England for use as studio props. Michael Lewis lists an entire inventory of costumes and objects making special note of the musical instruments which appear in the composition. Even more remarkable is his ability to attain compositional balance between the figures and the architectural space. Originating in the high and narrow walls, strong perspective lines recess down the corridor and sharply converge at the opposite sunlit entrance - an innovative pictorial device that accentuates the length of the cavernous bazaar. Lewis played with light like a magician delving into the complexities and patterns created by the dappling sunlight. Particularly beautiful atmospheric effects are achieved from the sunlight filtering through the open shafts in the ceiling illuminating the otherwise darkened bazaar. In preparation for his more polished studio works, Lewis made exhaustive drawings and impromptu sketches in Cairo, a number of which capture life among the bazaar merchants. Related sketches featuring rows of hanging garments and sumptuous textiles include The Bezestein Bazaar, Cairo and The Oriental Bazaar both in the Brinsley Ford Collection (figs. 2 and 3) and The Bazaar, El Khan Khalil, Cairo, in the National Gallery of Scotland (fig. 4). Not only do these drawings feature an interesting variety of figural compositions, they bring to light Lewis' skill as an architectural draughtsman. The existence of a nearly identical watercolor version of the present work, dated 1872, in the Cecil Higgins Art Gallery, Bedford (fig. 5) reveals a composition well-studied and carefully constructed with Lewis's characteristic technical precision and elegant style. For on-site sketches, these drawings are remarkable for their immediacy yet precision. A loose and rapidly sketched chalk drawing entitled Two men in Eastern costume (National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa) probably served as the model for the seated figures in the right foreground. With such distinguished provenance, the present work has formed the centerpiece of many distinguished English collections such as that of Lord Leverhulme and David Price, who owned another Lewis masterpiece, Lillium Auratum (Birmingham Art Gallery). The posthumous accolade that Lewis received is as strong today as it was during his lifetime. Fellow painter Edward Lear summed up best Lewis' achievements in a letter to his wife the year before the artist's death: "There have never been, and there will never be any works depicting Oriental life - more truly beautiful and excellent." During this time he based himself at the Alhambra or Seville, but he also made long tours around the country. In July 1832 he wrote to the Ambassador in Spain asking for a visa to be obtained for John Frederick Lewis, revealing that he was 'a clever artist, whose father I know well, has been recommended to me by Henry Wellesley. He is about to make a sort of picturesque tour of Spain, having orders for young ladies' albums and from divers book-sellers who are illustrating Lord Byron' (see Major-General Michael Lewis, C.B.E., John Frederick Lewis, R.A. 1805-1876, 1978, p.16). Lewis arrived in Madrid in the summer of 1832. From there he moved south to Grenada via Toledo and began his sketches and drawings of the Alhambra. He remained in Grenada until almost the end of the year, joining Richard Ford and his wife in Seville via Cordoba either late in November or early in December. The Fords had been looking forward to meeting Lewis and seeing his sketches. During the time Lewis stayed with them he gave lessons to Richard's wife, Harriet, and drew a number of portraits of his host and hostess, including an important watercolour, recorded as being in the Brinsley Ford Collection (ibid., fig.27, cat.no.197)

THE PROPERTY OF A LADY THE INTERIOR OF THE MOSQUE OF SANTA SOPHIA, CONSTANTINOPLE measurements note 37 by 54 cm., 14 1/2 by 21 1/4 in. signed and inscribed l.r.: St. Sophia. Constantinople/ J F Lewis pencil and watercolour, heightened with bodycolour PROVENANCE Presumably one of the drawings of the interior of Santa Sophia included in the sales of Lewis' work at Christie's on 4-5th May 1877 (one of lots 180, 254, 255, 268 and 269), 3rd May 1897 (lot 29) or 24th May 1909 (lots 137 and 143) NOTE Santa Sophia stands on the site of an earlier basilican church erected by Constantius II in 360 A.D. The Church was twice destroyed by fire and the present structure, was built in 532-37 by Emperor Justinian. With the Turkish Conquest of Constantinople in 1453, Santa Sophia became a mosque, and in subsequent years all the interior mosaics were obscured under coatings of plaster and painted ornament. The four minarets which rise at the outer corners of the structure, were added singly and at different times. The history of the mosque explains the varying styles of architecture inside the building. In the present work the great wooden doorway, for example, reveals the mosque's Christian past and is classical in style with a heavy architrave. This contrasts with the interior ceiling which is Ottoman and lavishly decorated with alternate red and white brick. The present watercolour depicting the interior of Santa Sophia dates from Lewis's sojourn in Constantinople from 1840-1841. After leaving Rome, Lewis travelled to Constantinople via Albania, Corfu, Janina, the Pindus Mountains, Patrass, Athens, the Gulf of Corinth and Smyrna. He remained there for a year, although made at least one excursion into Asia Minor as far as Brussa (Bursa), about one hundred miles south of the city. Whilst in Constantinople he met David Wilkie, who, when writing on 14th October 1840, to William Collins, R.A., said: 'We have encountered John Lewis from Greece and Smyrna. He is making a number of drawings. I said I was sure he would turn up on our route~He has been making the most clever drawings as usual.' (quoted in Major-General Michael Lewis, John Frederick Lewis, 1978, p.21). Lewis was fascinated by Constantinople's rich cultural heritage and on 22nd November 1840 accompanied Lady Londonderry (wife of the third Marquis of Londonderry whose portrait Lewis painted) on her tour of the city's mosques. In the words of Major-General Michael Lewis: 'Lewis must have been much moved, or, putting emotion at its lowest, at least much attracted by these great religious buildings of the East.' (John Frederick Lewis, 1978, p.21). Although he found all the mosques of interest, Lewis was particularly amazed, however, at the beauty of Santa Sophia and made a series of drawings of the interior, including the present work. Late in 1841, probably in November, he reluctantly left Constantinople and sailed for Egypt where he remained for ten years before returning to England.

NOTES John Frederick Lewis showed his first Royal Academy exhibit in 1821, well before he was 20 but he did not become a full Royal Academician until he was over 60. Unlike his friend Edwin Landseer, his career did not follow a straight course, as, in the meantime he was for over 30 years a member of the Old Water-Colour Society, being elected its President in 1855, only to resign less than three years later in order to devote more energy to the more lucrative medium of oil painting. The son of a successful engraver, Frederick Christian Lewis, whose trade he learnt, he gained early success as a painter of animals and sporting subjects, but, after a trip to Europe in 1826/27, he became more interested in the people and architecture of foreign places, finding watercolour a natural medium. A visit to Spain in 1832-34 reinforced these inclinations, and the watercolours and lithographs that resulted were widely acclaimed. Such success encouraged him to seek more exotic subjects further afield and from Italy in 1840 he journeyed via Alabania and Greece to Constantinople. After a year, he continued on to Egypt. Lewis then spent a decade, 1841-51, living and working in Cairo, at a time when few British artists had visited the city and even fewer had devoted attention to the everyday life of the people that inhabited it. Among the subjects especially favoured by Lewis were the streets and covered markets in the centre of the city, surrounding the impressive architecture of its Mamluk mosques and mausolea. He made a number of detailed but - perhaps deliberately - apparently unfinished pencil and watercolour sketches of these streets and bazaars, capturing the light and atmosphere of the vast spaces and accurately depicting the complex architectural features of the buildings with their intricately carved and banded stonework, wooden structures and textile awnings. These drawings were seen by Lewis's friend, the writer William Makepeace Thackeray, when he visited Cairo in 1844, towards the end of his tour around the eastern Mediterranean and they are mentioned in his later account of the trip, Notes of a Journey from Cornhill to Grand Cairo (1846). Describing his own astonishment at the scenes in Cairo that confronted him, he wrote: 'How to describe the beauty of the streets to you! - the fantastic splendour; the variety of the houses, and archways, and hanging roofs, and balconies, and porches; the delightful accidents of light and shade which chequer them; the noise, the bustle, the brilliancy of the crowd; the interminable vast bazaars with their barbaric splendour! There is a fortune to be made for painters in Cairo, and materials for a whole Academy of them. I never saw such a variety of architecture, of life, of picturesqueness, of brilliant colour, and light and shade. There is a picture in every street, and at every bazaar stall. Some of these, our celebrated water-colour painter, Mr Lewis, has produced with admirable truth and exceeding minuteness and beauty; but there is room for a hundred to follow him...'. A brilliant essayist and novelist, Thackeray's account of his journey combines fact and fiction in a typically idiosyncratic way. The description of his visit to Lewis that follows shortly after this passage is littered with double entendres aimed at a western audience already sated with a large body of popular travel literature. While Thackeray may deliberately have sensationalised his account of Lewis, much in it can be corroborated by the fragments of information that exist in letters from other European visitors and, read carefully, Thackeray's text reveals a great deal both about Lewis's life in Cairo and about the image of it that writer and artist wished to convey. Lewis, wrote Thackeray 'has established himself here in the most complete Oriental fashion' in a house, 'far away from the haunts of European civilisation, in the Arab quarter... situated in a cool, shady, narrow alley'. On entering the 'broad open court' he encountered 'the walls of his long, queer, many-windowed, many-galleried house' and was ushered into a 'hall of audience' with a ceiling 'carved, gilt, painted and embroidered with arabesques and choice sentences of Eastern writing'. At last 'J' appeared, but utterly changed from the sartorial frequenter of clubs he had known in London and Paris: 'A man - in a long yellow gown, with a long beard, somewhat tinged with grey, with his head shaved, and wearing on it first a white wadded cotton night-cap, second, a red tarboosh...' After a time however 'his oriental coolness and languor gave way to British cordiality' and he became again the amusing companion of former days. 'He has adapted himself outwardly, however, to the oriental life. When he goes abroad he rides a grey horse with red housings, and has two servants to walk beside him. He wears a very handsome grave costume of dark blue, consisting of an embroidered jacket and gaiters, and a pair of trousers, which would make a set of dresses for an English family. His beard curls nobly over his chest, his Damascus scimitar on his thigh. His red cap gives him a venerable and Bey-like appearance'. Thus attired, Lewis was well placed to roam the streets of Cairo and while his 'disguise' is unlikely to have fooled anybody it would at least have enabled him to observe the activities of the city's inhabitants at close quarters. Lewis lived a dual existence: he adopted the dress and customs of Cairo's Turkish elite, but retained many British habits, eating meat, as Thackeray noted, 'with an Infidel knife and fork' and drinking 'certain sherberts, prepared by the two great rivals, Hadji Hodson and Bass Bey'. He associated with the expatriate community, being described by Henry Abbott, another long-standing member of this group, as 'an excellent fellow, liked by everyone', he ordered tea from a British merchant in Alexandria and collected antiquities as well as the items of Egyptian costume, oriental procelain and artefacts that he later used extensively as props in his paintings. While conveying an impression of indolence - Thackery's 'languid Lotus-eater' - he was actively working to accumulate a large number of sketches and a few full-size compositions. While immersed in an Islamic society, he was at the same time engaged in the particularly European activity of recording and interpreting an 'alien' people for a 'home' audience. In 1851 Lewis returned to England, following the enormous acclaim with which his watercolour, The Hhareem, was received the previous year when it was exhibited at the Old Water-Colour Society. Armed with his store of sketches and his collection of costume and artefacts, he continued, over the next twenty-five years, to exhibit scenes of oriental life - bedouin with their camels in the desert, women gorgeously attired in interiors suffused with dappled light or in lush gardens surrounded by flowers, and traders, entertainers, scribes and other inhabitants of the bazaars and coffee-houses of Cairo. The present example is undated and is not known to have been exhibited, although it may be identifiable or be connected with either of two paintings that Lewis exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1862, A street in Cairo (no. 797) and Bazaar, Cairo (no. 815). In subject it relates closely to an oil painting exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1869, The seraff (money-changer), a doubtful coin; a scene in a Cairo bazaar (Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery). As in the latter painting, the man on the left, seated on a mastaba, turbanned and with a dark instead of a grey beard, holds up what appears to be a coin for examination, brought to him by the two veiled women in front of him. To their right stands the merchant with his lengths of cloth and his young black assistant waiting for the verdict on the disputed authenticity of the coin. Currency was a problem in Egypt in the late 1840s, as Lord Castlereagh, who was there in 1842, relates. Both Turkish and Egyptian money was in circulation, but since the hostilities between the Sultan of Turkey and the Pasha of Egypt, Muhammed Ali, Turkish currency was no longer legal tender. 'The consequence is', wrote Castlereagh, 'that every one who pays, endeavours to pass away some Turkish money, and in the old currency it is extremely difficult for a foreigner to tell the difference. Then again, many of the Pasha's pieces of gold have been depreciated, and clipped or split. These the people object to take at their value, and deduct half or a whole piastre, as they think expedient'. (Viscount Castlereagh, Journey to Damascus through Egypt, Nubia, Arabia Petrae, Palestine, and Syria, 1847, Vol. I, pp. 39-40). According to E.W. Lane, the great 19th century Arabist and author of An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836) 'seyrefees' or money-changers were often Jews and were held in high esteem for their integrity. Hence the disputants reliance on him for a fair judgement. The grouping of two women before an older, respected man, and the similar group which occupies the central space in the 1869 Doubtful Coin, may be derived from a similar arrangement of figures in David Wilkie's The Turkish Letter-Writer (Aberdeen Art Gallery and Museums), painted in 1840 while the artist was in Constantinople. Lewis, who knew and had a huge admiration for the older artist, was there at the same time. The two men communicated several times and on occasions sketched the same subjects, so it would not be surprising if one of the watercolours that Lewis exhibited soon after his return to England, The Arab Scribe - Cairo (1852; Private Collection), in which a similar group holds centre stage, was intended as a tribute to Wilkie, who had died at sea on the way home from the East, or that Lewis should re-employ with variations so successful a formula in later compositions. In A Doubtful Coin the narrative forms the central focus for the composition; whereas in the present painting it is part of a larger scene depicting the crowded thoroughfare of one of Cairo's busiest street markets. Indeed it seems to have been introduced at a fairly late stage since it is not present in the same format in the watercolour study for the painting (Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery). To acquire credibility as a painter of eastern scenes Lewis relied on an accumulation of realistic detail - architecture, costume, objects, gestures - and placed his protagonists in identifiable settings. The Ghuriyya would have been known to Lewis's public through one of the images in David Roberts's popular series of lithographs, Egypt and Nubia (1849, Vol III, Pl. 96, Bazaar of the Silk-Mercers, Cairo ), and would have been recognisable from the red and white banded walls and elaborate doorways and windows of the early 16th century mosque complex of Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri, the mausoleum (with the sabil and kuttab ) on the left and mosque- madrasa on the right facing each other across the street. The trader with his colourful silks and cottons and the bolts of fabric stacked up in the stalls against the buildings indicate the type of merchandise sold in the area. In order to achieve his goal of presenting an 'authentic' event in recognisable surroundings, the artist adds colour, movement and narrative detail to the architectural setting. Inevitably the fluidity and fine pencil work that makes the on-the-spot drawing (Witt Collection, Courtauld Institute of Art) so remarkable is sacrificed. A similar transformation takes place between the vertical format drawing of the Ghuriyya from the opposite direction (Opp‚ Collection, Tate, London) and the finished watercolour (signed and dated 1876; Sotheby's, 13 November 1997, lot 139) painted in the studio of his Surrey house approximately thirty years later. Nevertheless when its almost identical oil counterpart was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1877, the year after Lewis's death, with the title The street and mosque of the Ghoreeyah, Cairo, it was applauded in the Art Journal as 'showing all that exquisite detail, brilliant colouring and deft play of light for which his pictures were always so conspicuous' (1877, p. 269). (This painting was exhibited at the Fine Art Society, Recent Acquisitions, 1969, no. 71, went to an American private collection but was subsequently accidentally destroyed.) Also evident in the current painting, these are the qualities for which Lewis had been feted throughout his life. One of his staunchest champions was the influential art critic John Ruskin who hailed him in Praeterita as 'the painter of greatest power, next to Turner, in the English School'. Shorly before he died Lewis received a glowing tribute from his fellow artist, Edward Lear: 'There never have been & there never will be, any works depicting oriental life - more truly beautiful and excellent..... For besides the exquisite and conscientious workmanship, the subjects painted by J.F. Lewis were perfect as representations of real scenes and people' (letter to Lewis's wife Marian, 22 June 1875, Private Collection). A more critical 21st-century appraisal of Lewis's paintings might emphasise their presentation of a stereotypical view of Near Eastern life, but it should also appreciate the factual base in which each element of the composition is rooted and the absence of the moral undertones that inform so many other Victorian portrayals of Islamic society. portrayals of Islamic society.

NOTES Rudolf Ernst, born in Vienna in 1854, was the son of the architectural painter Leopold Ernst. After attending the Vienna Academy in 1869 and exhibiting in Munich he travelled to Italy in 1874. As early as 1876 Ernst decided to settle in Paris where he would exhibit at the Salon for the following six decades. Like his close friend Ludwig Deutsch, who also took French nationality, Ernst belongs to the second generation of Orientalist painters. The first generation, such as Delacroix, Vernet, Colin and Chass‚riau were inspired by political events such as Napoleon's conquest of Algeria and the liberation of Greece. Artists from the second half of the century such as G‚r“me, Bauernfeind, Deutsch and Ernst were more interested in depicting scenes from daily life. Ernst's first taste of the East was sparked by journeys to Moorish Spain, Morocco and Tunis in the second half of the 1880s, followed by a visit to Constantinople and Egypt in 1890. Ernst was especially impressed by Islamic ceramics and tiles and those in his collection reappear in many of his works. Ernst left Paris in 1905 to live in Fontenay-aux-Roses, where he decorated his home in an Ottoman style and lived among the objects which figured so largely in his paintings. Heavily influenced by the academic style of Jean-L‚on G‚r“me, both Ludwig Deutsch and Rudolf Ernst implemented the French master's exactitude in detail and intensity of colour. Yet Ernst's work differs fundamentally when compared to both G‚r“me and Deutsch, as his compositions are eclectic assemblies and include mixtures of objects from different sources such as Algeria, Tunisia, Turkey and Andalusian Spain. In Le Pacha, Ernst has juxtaposed the rich costumes of the central figures against the splendid Iznik blue and turquoise tiles which decorate the exterior of the mosque. Le Pacha formed part of an important collection which was largely acquired during the 1950s, and was a reflection of the owner's life-long interest as a traveller and writer in the Middle East. The collection was sold at Christie's London, 3 November 1977 and in addition to other paintings by Ernst, included important works by John Frederick Lewis, Ludwig Deutsch, Gustave Bauernfeind, and Jean-L‚on G‚r“me.

His beard curls nobly over his chest, his Damascus scimitar over his thigh.' Lewis's adaption and assimilation into Middle Eastern life was not merely cosmetic. He observed the busy streets of Cairo, and travelled through the deserts, entertained visitors from home and other expatriates as well as Egyptians. He seemed to have been acquainted with the ruling family of Cairo, and as a result painted one of its youngest members, Prince Hassan with his servant. NOTES Hailed as the greatest Orientalist painter the English School has ever produced, John Frederick Lewis left a surviving oeuvre of no less than two thousand sketches, watercolors, drawings and paintings. Born into an artistic family in 1805, the son of an engraver, Lewis was strongly urged by his father to join the family business. He envisioned himself as a painter and draughtsman however and his remarkable talent, evident at a young age, led him to exhibit at the Royal Academy in 1821 at the age of sixteen. He also earned membership to the prestigious Old Watercolor Society in 1827. After working in England and exhibiting around the country, it was not long before Lewis yearned to travel abroad. An early two-year sojourn in southern Spain and Morocco in 1832 would prove crucial to his future development as an Orientalist for it was here that he first encountered the intriguing new subject matter that would occupy him for the rest of his career. Enchanted by the sun-drenched Islamic mosques and the unique Moorish architecture of the Alhambra Palace, with its decorative courtyards, elegant archways and fountains, Lewis, fired up with enthusiasm, expanded his travels to Turkey and North Africa in pursuit of the "exotic". Yet unlike his other artistic contemporaries who made the traditional Orientalist pilgrimage, Lewis would spend nearly a decade in Egypt. The years spanning 1840-51 found the artist firmly entrenched in Arab life. Adopting the Arab dress and customs, his lengthy residence in Cairo as "a kind of aristocratic vagabond in the East" inspired some of his greatest compositions - a rich and varied repertory of works featuring harem beauties, rugged desert encampments and crowded Cairo streets and markets. The Bezestein Bazaar of El Khan Khalil, Cairo, is undoubtedly, the Orientalist tour de force of Lewis's late oeuvre. Painted in 1872 in his studio in Walton-on-Thames, it is one of his largest oils and represents the artist at the pinnacle of his creative powers. This celebrated composition - a stunning visual spectacle of a traditional Egyptian suk or marketplace - stands as a sort of artistic memoir of a life-long passion for Egypt, based on numerous sketches of people and places he encountered. Widely exhibited, the work drew positive reviews - the canvas's larger format representing a departure from the artist's usual smaller scale works. One reviewer wrote, "We have been so long accustomed to discourse with Mr. Lewis over his small pieces of microscopic finish, that anything larger brings with it a surprise for which there has been no preparation". He further praised the work as "a very spirited composition every passage of which is undoubtedly true". ( Art Journal, 1872, p. 282). But even before the R.A. show, his friend and fellow artist, Thomas Woolner would write, "You do not think so highly of your work as your admirers do, or you could not be surprised at any sum being offered for one of your chief pictures...very soon your works will be priceless" (Woolner to Lewis, 17 May 1874, Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection). Soon after the opening it is recorded that a collector from Glasgow made a private offer to buy the present work for the then generous sum of 10,000 gns. - an offer however stridently refused by the painting's first owner, David Price. It was Lewis's full immersion in Cairo life that not only enriched his understanding of the complex city but provided the impetus for his sensitive artistic portrayals. Dressed in native garb and at ease with the language, he easily disappeared into the crowd to observe and sketch for hours, later building up his oil compositions in his studio. Lewis was further compelled to live in the Ezbekiya quarter of Cairo, a residential area in the north of the city - "the most Ottoman quarter of Cairo" - far from the British ex-patriot community. There are many detailed accounts by friends who had a chance to observe the artist's lifestyle as an oriental pasha (fig. 1). After a visit to Lewis's residence, friend William Thackeray provides one of the most colorful descriptions: First we came into a broad open court, with a covered gallery running along one side of it. A camel was reclining on the grass there; near him was a gazelle...and a numerous brood of hens and chickens, who furnish his liberal table. On the opposite side of the covered gallery rose up the walls of his long queer many-windowed, many-galleried house...while I was examining the strange apartments and all its contents, my respect and awe for the owner increased vastly. So profound was Lewis's transformation into an oriental pasha that Thackeray failed to recognize his friend. Lewis entered dressed "in a long yellow gown, with a long beard, somewhat tinged with grey, with his head shaved, and wearing on it first a white wadded cotton nightcap, second, a red tarboosh. It was some time, as the Americans say, before I could 'realise' the semillant J. of old times" (Thackeray, Notes of a Journey from Cornhill to Cairo, 1846, pp. 377-81). The district of Khan el-Khalili, home to a vast network of markets, was one of the most important trading centers in Cairo. Also known as the Turkish bazaar during the Ottoman period, the complex dates back to the fourteenth century when it was built by the Emir Djaharks el-Khalili in the heart of the Fatimid city in medieval Cairo. Bazaar culture has always been a central component of Arab life throughout the centuries, important not only to the commercial livelihood of the country but as a focal point for community gatherings. In larger cities, markets were defined by their quarter and were clustered around a mosque and hamman or public bath. During Lewis's residence, in the mid-19th Century, Egypt under the Mamluk dynasty flourished as a trading center. From the documentary architectural evidence afforded by present work, Caroline H. Williams has recently confirmed that the market Lewis has depicted here is in fact the great Ghuriyya market, the main cloth market of Cairo and a southern extension of El Khan Khalili. Named after the ruling 16th Century Sultan Al-Ghuri, the complex is anchored by two buildings that sit opposite each other on the main ceremonial street of medieval Cairo - the Mosque-Madrasa to the east and the Mausoleum-Sabil-Kuttab to the west. These bustling streets ranked as favorite areas among Western artists such as David Roberts and Owen B. Carter who were among the first to depict the Ghuriyya. In 1851 Lewis's Street and Mosque of the Gouriah (Lewis, no. 516) shows a view of the more open markets running along the street. The present work is unique in that Lewis has chosen to depict the less touristed covered Ghuriyya market located to the west of the Mosque Madrasa building. Confronted by the exhausting maze of the grand market, Lewis successfully captures the energy of a bustling Arab bazaar. In contrast to his earlier market scenes that emphasized smaller compositional groups or individual portrayals of merchants, ( In the Bezestein Bazaar, Cairo, 1860; (Lewis, 1978, no. 582) and A Cairo Bazaar; The Dellal ; Lewis, 1978, no. 618), the present composition is his grandest and most animated depiction of the interior of a bazaar. A long narrow structure with vaulted ceilings, the market is defined by rows of stalls where merchants display their fine silks and fabrics. While much of the day was spent hawking goods to clients, there was ample time for socializing. In the foreground of the composition Lewis has set up a dialogue between the two groups of wealthy merchants who, during a musical interlude, engage in smoking, eating and idle conversation. Stylistically, the present work represents the successful fusion of Lewis's skillful draughtsmanship with his ongoing experimentation with color and atmospheric effects. Although Lewis drew considerable praise for his virtuoso handling of the watercolor medium, he was equally skilled with oils and in the 1850s it became his preferred media, not to mention more commerically valuable. Whatever the medium, Lewis strove for a highly polished surface. As shown in the present work, the brushwork denotes a precision and delicacy and, when coupled with the robust red, blue, and green hues that contrast against the darkened interior, the overall effect is mesmerizing. Lewis crowds the majority of the merchants into the foreground, yet does not subordinate detail to the quantity of figures. From the intricately patterned fabrics to other decorative embellishments such as the hookah and the bowl of freshly cut fruit, Lewis lavishes his attentions on the exquisite dress and shop trinkets. The degree of detail achieved is not surprising due to his immense personal collection of objects, instruments and clothing which he brought back to England for use as studio props. Michael Lewis lists an entire inventory of costumes and objects making special note of the musical instruments which appear in the composition. Even more remarkable is his ability to attain compositional balance between the figures and the architectural space. Originating in the high and narrow walls, strong perspective lines recess down the corridor and sharply converge at the opposite sunlit entrance - an innovative pictorial device that accentuates the length of the cavernous bazaar. Lewis played with light like a magician delving into the complexities and patterns created by the dappling sunlight. Particularly beautiful atmospheric effects are achieved from the sunlight filtering through the open shafts in the ceiling illuminating the otherwise darkened bazaar. In preparation for his more polished studio works, Lewis made exhaustive drawings and impromptu sketches in Cairo, a number of which capture life among the bazaar merchants. Related sketches featuring rows of hanging garments and sumptuous textiles include The Bezestein Bazaar, Cairo and The Oriental Bazaar both in the Brinsley Ford Collection (figs. 2 and 3) and The Bazaar, El Khan Khalil, Cairo, in the National Gallery of Scotland (fig. 4). Not only do these drawings feature an interesting variety of figural compositions, they bring to light Lewis' skill as an architectural draughtsman. The existence of a nearly identical watercolor version of the present work, dated 1872, in the Cecil Higgins Art Gallery, Bedford (fig. 5) reveals a composition well-studied and carefully constructed with Lewis's characteristic technical precision and elegant style. For on-site sketches, these drawings are remarkable for their immediacy yet precision. A loose and rapidly sketched chalk drawing entitled Two men in Eastern costume (National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa) probably served as the model for the seated figures in the right foreground. With such distinguished provenance, the present work has formed the centerpiece of many distinguished English collections such as that of Lord Leverhulme and David Price, who owned another Lewis masterpiece, Lillium Auratum (Birmingham Art Gallery). The posthumous accolade that Lewis received is as strong today as it was during his lifetime. Fellow painter Edward Lear summed up best Lewis' achievements in a letter to his wife the year before the artist's death: "There have never been, and there will never be any works depicting Oriental life - more truly beautiful and excellent." # GORE, SPENCER FREDERICK (1878-1914)

Plaque erected in **2017** by **English Heritage** at **31 Mornington Crescent, London, NW1 7RE, London Borough of Camden**

![Image 4: Circular blue plaque to Spencer Gore](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/find-a-plaque/blue-plaques-f-j/gore-plaque.jpg?w=350&h=350&mode=crop&scale=both&cache=always&quality=60&anchor=middlecenter&WebsiteVersion=20200219)![Image 5: View of terraced brick house with blue plaque mounted at 1st floor level](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/find-a-plaque/blue-plaques-f-j/gore-house.jpg?w=350&h=350&mode=crop&scale=both&cache=always&quality=60&anchor=middlecenter&WebsiteVersion=20200219)

SPENCER FREDERICK GORE 1878-1914 Painter lived and worked here 1909-1912

Material

The artist Spencer Gore was at the cutting edge of British art in the early 20th century. A close friend of Walter Sickert, he was a founding member of the Fitzroy Street Group, the Camden Town Group and the London Group. He is commemorated with a blue plaque at 31 Mornington Crescent, where he lived from about 1909 until 1912.

![Image 6: A painting, post-impressionist in style, depicting a seated man in dark suit jacket with short brown hair against a backdrop of yellow walls, flowers and a purple framed painting](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/find-a-plaque/blue-plaques-f-j/gore-self-portrait.jpg?maxwidth=1080&mode=none&scale=downscale&quality=60&anchor=&WebsiteVersion=20200219)

 A self-portrait by Spencer Gore painted in 1914, shortly before his death from pneumonia  © National Portrait Gallery, London

## ARTISTIC DEVELOPMENT

Gore attended the Slade School of Fine Art from 1897 until 1901, where he was introduced to English impressionism by his painting tutor [Philip Wilson Steer](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/philip-wilson-steer/). While there he made lasting friendships with Albert Rutherston and Harold Gilman, [Augustus John](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/augustus-john/) and Wyndham Lewis. His most important friendship, however, was to be with Walter Sickert, whom he met while on a painting trip to France in 1904.

Both men lived in London from 1905 onwards, and Sickert became an influential artistic guide and champion for Gore. Gore’s painting style responded to the broken colour and handling of the French Impressionists. He would sketch and paint, sometimes in Sickert’s studio, or in the music halls and streets of London. His subjects reflected the mix of London’s social culture portraying the streets and homes of working men and women. In the hands of Gore, Sickert wrote, dreary and hopeless scenes were ‘transformed into loveliness’.

## FROM FITZROY TO CAMDEN

In 1907 Gore helped Sickert set up the Fitzroy Street Group, an informal collection of artists who gathered on Saturday afternoons at 19 Fitzroy Street, Fitzrovia. The first members included two women, Ethel Sands and her partner Nan Hudson – plus Harold Gilman and Malcolm Drummond, with [Robert Bevan](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/robert-polhill-bevan/) and Charles Ginner joining them after 1908. Sickert defined the Group’s purpose as providing the opportunity for younger artists to show 'Little pictures for Little Patrons’ – affordable pictures at a scale that would fit homes rather than for the grander exhibition shows, and to accustom people to seeing modern and innovative works.

In 1911 Gore and Sickert set up another artists’ group: the men-only Camden Town Group. The 16 artists, who included Wyndham Lewis, Lucien Pissarro and [Duncan Grant](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/vanessa-bell-duncan-grant/ "Duncan Grant"), had little stylistic bond between them, but shared the ambition to respond to modernist ideals and truthfully observe the social and cultural life of modern Britain.

## MORNINGTON CRESCENT

In 1909 Gore moved to 31 Mornington Crescent in Camden Town, where he is now commemorated with a blue plaque. The blue plaque to Sickert is also located nearby at 6 Mornington Crescent, where he lived from 1905 until about 1908, shortly before Gore’s arrival.

The three years that Gore lived here saw him progress into an artist of ability and innovation. One of his four works shown in the first Camden Town Group exhibition was Mornington Crescent, a view painted from his window across the gardens to Hampstead Road. At least eight works in total were painted here: two showing the interior of the comfortable sitting room he shared with his landlord and six documenting either views from his window, or from within the residents’ private garden. Unfortunately the view Gore painted has been lost. The private gardens are now occupied by the Carreras Cigarette Factory, the Egyptian-style façade of which faces the Hampstead Road.

In 1926 the artist Walter Bayes wrote to _The Times_ to suggest that a new row of shops about to be built in Mornington Crescent should be called ‘Spencer Gore’s Grove’. Bayes recalled Gore ‘standing at his easel in the most inclement weathers painting so many charming pictures there to the accompaniment of the hum of the trams’.

Gore moved out of number 31 in 1912 after his marriage to Mary Johanna Kerr (1889–1968), known as Mollie. The couple moved to Richmond the following year, and from there Gore worked to bring together new artists for the Camden Town Group’s successor, the London Group. Their first exhibition in 1914 was to be Gore’s swansong: he contracted influenza which turned to pneumonia, and died on 27 March, aged 35.

# GORE, SPENCER FREDERICK (1878-1914)

Plaque erected in **2017** by **English Heritage** at **31 Mornington Crescent, London, NW1 7RE, London Borough of Camden**

![Image 4: Circular blue plaque to Spencer Gore](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/find-a-plaque/blue-plaques-f-j/gore-plaque.jpg?w=350&h=350&mode=crop&scale=both&cache=always&quality=60&anchor=middlecenter&WebsiteVersion=20200219)![Image 5: View of terraced brick house with blue plaque mounted at 1st floor level](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/find-a-plaque/blue-plaques-f-j/gore-house.jpg?w=350&h=350&mode=crop&scale=both&cache=always&quality=60&anchor=middlecenter&WebsiteVersion=20200219)

SPENCER FREDERICK GORE 1878-1914 Painter lived and worked here 1909-1912

Material

Ceramic

The artist Spencer Gore was at the cutting edge of British art in the early 20th century. A close friend of Walter Sickert, he was a founding member of the Fitzroy Street Group, the Camden Town Group and the London Group. He is commemorated with a blue plaque at 31 Mornington Crescent, where he lived from about 1909 until 1912.

![Image 6: A painting, post-impressionist in style, depicting a seated man in dark suit jacket with short brown hair against a backdrop of yellow walls, flowers and a purple framed painting](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/find-a-plaque/blue-plaques-f-j/gore-self-portrait.jpg?maxwidth=1080&mode=none&scale=downscale&quality=60&anchor=&WebsiteVersion=20200219)

 A self-portrait by Spencer Gore painted in 1914, shortly before his death from pneumonia  © National Portrait Gallery, London

## ARTISTIC DEVELOPMENT

Gore attended the Slade School of Fine Art from 1897 until 1901, where he was introduced to English impressionism by his painting tutor [Philip Wilson Steer](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/philip-wilson-steer/). While there he made lasting friendships with Albert Rutherston and Harold Gilman, [Augustus John](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/augustus-john/) and Wyndham Lewis. His most important friendship, however, was to be with Walter Sickert, whom he met while on a painting trip to France in 1904.

Both men lived in London from 1905 onwards, and Sickert became an influential artistic guide and champion for Gore. Gore’s painting style responded to the broken colour and handling of the French Impressionists. He would sketch and paint, sometimes in Sickert’s studio, or in the music halls and streets of London. His subjects reflected the mix of London’s social culture portraying the streets and homes of working men and women. In the hands of Gore, Sickert wrote, dreary and hopeless scenes were ‘transformed into loveliness’.

## FROM FITZROY TO CAMDEN

In 1907 Gore helped Sickert set up the Fitzroy Street Group, an informal collection of artists who gathered on Saturday afternoons at 19 Fitzroy Street, Fitzrovia. The first members included two women, Ethel Sands and her partner Nan Hudson – plus Harold Gilman and Malcolm Drummond, with [Robert Bevan](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/robert-polhill-bevan/) and Charles Ginner joining them after 1908. Sickert defined the Group’s purpose as providing the opportunity for younger artists to show 'Little pictures for Little Patrons’ – affordable pictures at a scale that would fit homes rather than for the grander exhibition shows, and to accustom people to seeing modern and innovative works.

In 1911 Gore and Sickert set up another artists’ group: the men-only Camden Town Group. The 16 artists, who included Wyndham Lewis, Lucien Pissarro and [Duncan Grant](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/vanessa-bell-duncan-grant/ "Duncan Grant"), had little stylistic bond between them, but shared the ambition to respond to modernist ideals and truthfully observe the social and cultural life of modern Britain.

## MORNINGTON CRESCENT

In 1909 Gore moved to 31 Mornington Crescent in Camden Town, where he is now commemorated with a blue plaque. The blue plaque to Sickert is also located nearby at 6 Mornington Crescent, where he lived from 1905 until about 1908, shortly before Gore’s arrival.

The three years that Gore lived here saw him progress into an artist of ability and innovation. One of his four works shown in the first Camden Town Group exhibition was Mornington Crescent, a view painted from his window across the gardens to Hampstead Road. At least eight works in total were painted here: two showing the interior of the comfortable sitting room he shared with his landlord and six documenting either views from his window, or from within the residents’ private garden. Unfortunately the view Gore painted has been lost. The private gardens are now occupied by the Carreras Cigarette Factory, the Egyptian-style façade of which faces the Hampstead Road.

In 1926 the artist Walter Bayes wrote to _The Times_ to suggest that a new row of shops about to be built in Mornington Crescent should be called ‘Spencer Gore’s Grove’. Bayes recalled Gore ‘standing at his easel in the most inclement weathers painting so many charming pictures there to the accompaniment of the hum of the trams’.

Gore moved out of number 31 in 1912 after his marriage to Mary Johanna Kerr (1889–1968), known as Mollie. The couple moved to Richmond the following year, and from there Gore worked to bring together new artists for the Camden Town Group’s successor, the London Group. Their first exhibition in 1914 was to be Gore’s swansong: he contracted influenza which turned to pneumonia, and died on 27 March, aged 35.

The son of a British Doctor who worked in Cannes in the South of France, Charles Ginner (1878–1952) only came to London in 1910 to serve on the hanging committee of the Allied Artists Association's exhibition that year. Meeting Spencer Gore and Harold Gilman, he quickly joined the Camden Town Group, then the London Group and Cumberland Market Group. Only he amongst the Camden Town Group really painted places in central London that in the period up to the First World War he would have been seeing for the first time. _Developed in association with Grant Waters, Art Detective Group Leader: South East England, East England and the Midlands._

# Artists and places: Charles Ginner in central London

[David Saywell, Head of Digital Assets](https://artuk.org/discover/profile/david-saywell-head-of-digital-assets)

Link copied to clipboard!

The son of a British Doctor who worked in Cannes in the South of France, Charles Ginner (1878–1952) only came to London in 1910 to serve on the hanging committee of the Allied Artists Association's exhibition that year. Meeting Spencer Gore and Harold Gilman, he quickly joined the Camden Town Group, then the London Group and Cumberland Market Group. Only he amongst the Camden Town Group really painted places in central London that in the period up to the First World War he would have been seeing for the first time. _Developed in association with Grant Waters, Art Detective Group Leader: South East England, East England and the Midlands._

# Three Halls and a Hospital – City of London Blue Plaques

16 Replies

If you have walked the street of the City of London, you may possibly have noticed one of the City of London blue plaques.

The City of London Corporation have their own plaques to mark the locations of lost churches, hospitals, halls of the Guilds of the City, famous names and events etc. Whilst English Heritage are responsible for the circular blue plaque outside of the City, within the City, the rectangular blue plaque is the standard, and there are around 170 to be found.

New plaques are still occasionally installed, however the process is slow as there is approximately five years for a successful application, with many authorities being consulted regarding the subject of the proposed plaque, along with the owner of the building on which the plaque will be installed.

They display a minimal amount of information – “Site of”, “Near this spot” etc. followed by a name of a building or institution. Where an individual’s name is the subject of a plaque, there is usually a small amount of additional information, although limited by the standard dimensions of the plaque.

One of my many photographic side projects has been to photograph these over the years, so to start a very occasional series of posts on the City’s plaques, for today’s post, the story of three halls and a hospital.

## Upholders’ Hall

The first plaque is not that obvious. Walk up towards St Paul’s Cathedral, along Peter’s Hill from Queen Victoria Street, and towards ground level on one of the buildings on the right, partly covered by some planting, is the plaque recording the site of Upholders’ Hall (see bottom right corner in following photo):

[![Image 2: Upholders Hall](https://alondoninheritance.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Blue-Plaques-2-scaled.jpg)](https://alondoninheritance.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Blue-Plaques-2-scaled.jpg)
Site of Upholders’ Hall, destroyed in the Great Fire 1666:

[![Image 3: Upholders Hall](https://alondoninheritance.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Blue-Plaques-1-1024x682.jpg)](https://alondoninheritance.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Blue-Plaques-1-scaled.jpg)
My go to book on the City’s Guilds is _“The Armorial Bearings of the Guilds of London”_, by John Bromley and published in 1960. The book provides an overview of each Guild or Company, along with their coat of arms. The book describes an Upholder as:

_“An upholder, or upholster, was originally one who dealt in soft furnishings which involved the use of stuffing to ‘uphold’ them”._

Therefore an upholder is an upholster, and the origin of the word upholster which is now generally used as a verb, is from the act of stuffing an item of furniture.

The Upholders’ formed around 1360, and as with most of the City’s Guilds at the time, their main role was to regulate their craft and ensure that goods produced met certain standards and quality, and were sold at a fair price (to both the customer and other craftsman to minimise any undercutting of members of the Guild). In 1474, the scope of the Upholders’ included _“feather-beds, pillows, mattresses, cushions, quilts, curtains and spervers”_ (a sperver was the canopy over a bed).

The scope of the Upholders’ was enlarged in 1495 to provide them with powers of inspection and control _“throughout the kingdom”_, and the manufacture of clothing also came within their scope, including mourning clothes which led the Upholders to be spoken of as:

_“The upholder, rueful harbinger of death, Waits with impatience for the dying breadth”_

As the plaque describes, their Hall was close to Peter’s Hill and was destroyed during the Great Fire of 1666. As with a number of Guilds, their hall was not rebuilt and they were able to use the halls of other Guilds for their ceremonial events.

The Worshipful Company of Upholders, as they are now known, is still in existence. As with many of the City’s Guilds or Companies, they lost their regulatory powers during the 19th century, and are now mainly a charitable organisation, but still have strong links with those in the upholstery business and upholstery trade organisations.

The Upholders were granted their Coat of Arms in 1465, and Charles I granted a Royal Charter which was lost during the fire in 1666.

The coat of arms of the Upholders is shown below:

[![Image 4: City of London Blue Plaques](https://alondoninheritance.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Blue-Plaques-11-915x1024.jpg)](https://alondoninheritance.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Blue-Plaques-11.jpg)
The book has a rather complex description of the coat of arms, which seems to reduce to three canopies (or spervers) with one covering the lamb of god and a cross (for religious significance) with the lamb sitting on a pillow of gold. Both the canopy and pillow being products of the Upholders trade.
