## The Evolution of Blue Plaques

Whenever I stop to think about it, blue plaques are truly amazing.

Although they began in London, now anyone who looks up all over the UK is treated to a clue about extraordinary contributions from former residents.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MD1n!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F69bcaa15-e6fb-4245-a32a-d94f4684a8da_2332x2505.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MD1n!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F69bcaa15-e6fb-4245-a32a-d94f4684a8da_2332x2505.jpeg)

_In front of Dame Millicent Fawcett’s blue plaque on a ‘Bloomsbury’s Inspiring Women’ walk!_

## But whose idea was it?

Along the stuccoed terraces of Belgravia, at 16 Eaton Place you can find a small blue plaque for William Ewart (1798-1869).

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wc3O!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F55e8f6de-4ca9-4692-9cdf-c0d980cb643c_768x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wc3O!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F55e8f6de-4ca9-4692-9cdf-c0d980cb643c_768x1024.jpeg)

_**[Blue Plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/william-ewart/)** at 16 Eaton Place, Belgravia – Image by **[Spudgun77](https://www.flickr.com/photos/24701549@N07/15699260348/)** CC BY 2.0_

A politician and reformer, what this plaque _doesn’t_ tell you is that the idea for blue plaques came from him!

I doubt that when William stood up in the House of Commons on 17 July 1863 anyone predicted the legacy **[his words](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/1863-07-17/debates/f5463ba6-1538-4b64-9ef7-cd1b3b641df5/CommonsChamber)** would have.

Might it be practical, William posed, _“to have inscribed on those houses in London which been inhabited by celebrated persons, the names of such persons.”_?

He continued to give possible examples of “_how rich the metropolis was in such associations”_ including John Milton at 19 York Street Westminster, Isaac Newton and Joshua Reynolds off Leicester Square and Dr Johnson in Gough Square.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9gBZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5be87f00-a4c3-4bfb-a39d-8a30ed49ae84_735x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9gBZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5be87f00-a4c3-4bfb-a39d-8a30ed49ae84_735x1024.jpeg)

_Action shot of me during a **[Fleet Street](https://lookup.london/walking-tours/fleet-street-walking-tour/)** walk in front of Dr Johnson’s plaque_

He concluded that _“other nations were in the habit of preserving memorial of their great men”_ and London should too.

What a great idea, right? But who could make it a reality…

## The Society of Arts

Someone who was paying attention was Sir Henry Cole, first Director of the Victoria and Albert Museum and the co-organiser of the Great Exhibition of 1851.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!F32b!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc286d98a-516d-413d-8055-3259204921d6_721x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!F32b!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc286d98a-516d-413d-8055-3259204921d6_721x1024.png)

_A mosaic featuring Henry Cole on the Ceramic Staircase in the V&A_

In July 1863 Cole wrote a letter to the journal of the Society of Arts (later the Royal Society of Arts or RSA) mentioning the parliamentary debate. He proposed that the RSA should take this scheme forward:

_“It seems to me a proper subject for the Society of Arts to consider. The object in view is of public interest, and refers especially to celebrities in arts, science, manufactures, commerce and literature.”_

Henry Cole’s blue plaque was **[erected](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/henry-cole/)** in 1991 opposite the V&A.

The Treasurer of the RSA was a man called George Bartley, someone keen to preserve London’s history and who already concerned that too much of the city’s heritage was being torn down in the early 1860s. He commissioned the Staffordshire potter, Herbert Minton to create two blue, circular ceramic plaques.

One was for the birthplace of Lord Byron on Holles Street and the other for Napoleon III who lived for a time on King Street.

These were erected in 1867 as London’s first blue plaques but now only one survives.

If you want to find London’s oldest blue plaque you just need to look up at 3 King Street in St James’s.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rYfg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8e71b571-7730-4222-ab34-e10c460fff99_992x991.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rYfg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8e71b571-7730-4222-ab34-e10c460fff99_992x991.jpeg)

The RSA managed the blue plaque scheme until 1901 but their plaques weren’t always blue, in fact the majority of the 35 erected were a terracotta brown.

You can easily identify the RSA plaques, not only by their matte finish but by the decorative edging that spells out ‘Erected by The Society of Arts’ interspaced with interlaced curved lines and little crosses.

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BZVA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedfed856-f7c5-4959-b67e-85ab35d1d3e9_979x979.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BZVA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedfed856-f7c5-4959-b67e-85ab35d1d3e9_979x979.jpeg)

_John Dryden’s RSA plaque (that needs some tlc) on Gerrard Street in Chinatown_

A brown **[plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/dr-samuel-johnson/)** for Dr Samuel Johnson was erected in 1876 at 17 Gough Square, one of the people originally suggested by William Ewart back in 1863.

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!haQc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffedc07e2-7c53-4db1-961f-ca077cc4e894_1080x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!haQc!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffedc07e2-7c53-4db1-961f-ca077cc4e894_1080x1080.jpeg)

This plaque off Fleet Street is also unique because it’s the only _official_ blue plaque within the Square Mile.

## City of London Plaques

True to form, The City of London decided around 1879 that they would do things differently and manage their own scheme of plaques.

City of London plaques are still blue, but square and they tend to focus more on former buildings and institutions over individuals.

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NiIs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff8c1e0b4-ada5-43b2-80a9-c033f76b80a0_676x519.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NiIs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff8c1e0b4-ada5-43b2-80a9-c033f76b80a0_676x519.jpeg)

By my latest count there were 182 City of London plaques. Out of these only 38 commemorate actual people (with a _whopping_ 3 of those being women).

If you’re curious as to which three women are commemorated, they are Elizabeth Fry, **[Susanna Wesley](https://lookup.london/spital-yard-susanna-wesley/)** and Mary Harris Smith (the first woman to qualify as an accountant).

You can view an interactive map of the City of London Plaques **[here](https://www.mapping.cityoflondon.gov.uk/geocortex/mapping/?viewer=compass&runworkflowbyid=Switch_layer_themes&LayerTheme=Show%20the%20Heritage%20Estate%20layers)**.

From 1901 a new body took over the running of the blue plaque scheme…

## London County Council

The London County Council who were the local governing body for London from 1889 until 1965.

It was under them that the scheme really got going with hundreds of new plaques popping up across London.

[![Image 13](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xd-E!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5d71c076-b44a-4fbf-8d87-6a66cd88eafb_1080x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xd-E!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5d71c076-b44a-4fbf-8d87-6a66cd88eafb_1080x1080.jpeg)

_Thomas de Quincey’s Covent Garden plaque which spells his name wrong! It’s missing an ‘e’_

If you enjoy a bit of hard data, between 1903 and 1965 they erected 250 plaques and then under its new name (the Greater London Council) they put up a further 262.

At first the LCC have a similar design to the RSC plaques, with a decorative border and then the initials LCC at the top.

[![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fu8S!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6999e400-3902-4179-ad4e-437cc3c57525_1105x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fu8S!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6999e400-3902-4179-ad4e-437cc3c57525_1105x1080.png)

_3 Prime Ministers for the price of 1 in St James’s Square!_

They also experimented with a few different designs, one of the prettiest can still be found on Beak Street in Soho

[![Image 15](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AJ5Q!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F978be447-7b4a-4182-b821-b9822ecb3ee5_900x660.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AJ5Q!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F978be447-7b4a-4182-b821-b9822ecb3ee5_900x660.png)

_Love the succinct but charming wording on this **[plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/mary-hughes/)** at 71 Vallace Road, Whitechapel_

Over time the LCC and and then GLC blue plaques start to appear much more uniform.

They have the brighter blue colour and sheen as well as a more standardised format for the text. Typically it has the person’s name and their dates alongside a few words to describe them underneath.

[![Image 16](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Byr6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F81b2233a-53ac-41c7-8e78-a6c46b2025fa_923x924.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Byr6!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F81b2233a-53ac-41c7-8e78-a6c46b2025fa_923x924.jpeg)

_Love the succinct but charming wording on this **[plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/mary-hughes/)** at 71 Vallance Road, Whitechapel_

As blue plaques proliferated across the capital so did their prestige and power.

At 48 Doughty Street today you can find the **[Charles Dickens Museum](https://dickensmuseum.com/)**. In 1903 a LCC plaque was unveiled on the writer’s former home well before it became a museum (in 1925) and probably helped save the home from major renovation.

In the cases of blue plaques for Vincent Van Gogh, Oscar Wilde and D.H. Lawrence all helped to ensure that the homes were preserved for posterity rather than face demolition.

[![Image 17](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2LTP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8135c615-8d3e-4cd5-81df-fdc323fa0b18_1432x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2LTP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8135c615-8d3e-4cd5-81df-fdc323fa0b18_1432x1080.png)

_The LCC plaque – with beautiful decorative features – outside the Charles Dickens Museum_

One of my favourite plaques from the Greater London Council era is Edward Johnston’s plaque in Chiswick. Look properly and there’s something _off_ about it.

[![Image 18](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8mi6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1afcbd26-3815-4c37-9442-6f5f9b51f40c_492x492.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8mi6!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1afcbd26-3815-4c37-9442-6f5f9b51f40c_492x492.jpeg)

It was Johnston that created the famous typeface still used by Transport For London today and this is the only plaque that uses that special font!

But another great one to spot arrives in 1986, when one of the final blue plaques they unveiled was to… themselves!

[![Image 19](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rE59!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1bab5c77-9871-4c62-88a3-2fb6cacdf62e_1062x862.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rE59!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1bab5c77-9871-4c62-88a3-2fb6cacdf62e_1062x862.jpeg)

An unusual design with an extra decorative border on **[County Hall](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/london-county-council/)**.

## English Heritage

Since 1986 the Blue Plaque Scheme has been managed by English Heritage, where often you can spot their logo at the bottom.

[![Image 20](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G-nT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F931711f9-c2d1-40e4-a708-34643c1e7b6a_1036x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G-nT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F931711f9-c2d1-40e4-a708-34643c1e7b6a_1036x1080.jpeg)

This charming [blue plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/luke-howard/) is in Bruce Grove, Tottenham

Today all English Heritage blue plaques are still made by hand. For over 40 years they were made by Frank and Sue Ashworth but Sue sadly died in 2026. You can watch a lovely video of them working on the plaque for Freddie Mercury **[here](https://youtu.be/BAmnwsVfu1U?si=gSbVOcUi2tPsdBnx)**.

The immense task and privilege now falls to Ned Heywood and Julia Land from Ned Heywood Heritage Ceramics. Since 2018 they have been making ceramic plaques from their base in Chepstow.

In the decades that English Heritage have managed blue plaques, they’ve erected hundreds more plaques across London and now there are well over 1,000 total.

In recent years they’ve concentrated on honouring a more diverse selection of Londoners. In 2016 less than 4% of plaques represented Black or Asian people and only 15% of the total number of plaques were for women and you can read more about their plans on the English Heritage website **here**.

[![Image 21](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!B8dD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F588a336c-bade-49e8-9cff-f771598ef776_861x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!B8dD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F588a336c-bade-49e8-9cff-f771598ef776_861x1080.jpeg)

_A double whammy in Bloomsbury where Gower Street has two blue plaque naming three remarkable women!_

[![Image 22](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m4uZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcd511f38-cb80-4888-94fd-32cb0e7989c6_1075x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m4uZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcd511f38-cb80-4888-94fd-32cb0e7989c6_1075x1080.jpeg)

## Who Gets a Blue Plaque?

Anyone can nominate a person to receive an English Heritage blue plaque.

[![Image 23](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Nuyj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb3775e54-9bac-4781-bd91-55ea78d856a9_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Nuyj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb3775e54-9bac-4781-bd91-55ea78d856a9_1024x1024.png)

_The LCC plaque for John Howard on Great Ormond Street in Bloomsbury_

These proposals are considered by a panel, but the general rules are that 1) the person has to have been dead for 20 years and 2) they have made a ‘positive contribution to human welfare and happiness’.

It’s also important that the person commemorated has a longstanding association with the building (they didn’t just stay overnight one time!) and it helps if the building is the original.

You can read more about submitting a blue plaque request **[here](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/propose-a-plaque/)**.

## Green and other ‘Unofficial’ Plaques

It’s not just the City of London that wanted to celebrate local history via their own scheme.

Many other London boroughs or independent societies have their own versions and English Heritage **[lists](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/propose-plaque/other-plaque-schemes.pdf)** 32 different schemes from which here are just a few examples of the variety you can find across London.

[![Image 24](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9J5-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89c8d101-7495-48ad-8686-06650a6e15b1_625x651.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9J5-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89c8d101-7495-48ad-8686-06650a6e15b1_625x651.jpeg)

_One of the Islington Council People’s Plaques (Est. 2010)_

[![Image 25](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IF8m!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3eff0c57-0d73-4344-beeb-990c86102248_768x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IF8m!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3eff0c57-0d73-4344-beeb-990c86102248_768x1024.jpeg)

_A Bow Heritage Trail plaque, unveiled in the 1990s_

The City of Westminster launched their own scheme in 1991 with the criteria of being eminent, deserving of recognition and reasonably well known. Like English Heritage there also has to have been a sufficient amount of time since their death to ensure their lasting legacy.

[![Image 26](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V4xy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75adfb04-2d8d-4f64-87a6-a0a7fa38ae4e_1024x952.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V4xy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75adfb04-2d8d-4f64-87a6-a0a7fa38ae4e_1024x952.png)

_Jeremy Bentham’s plaque on Queen Anne’s Gate, Westminster_

Many of the Westminster plaques are sponsored, the main sponsor being named at the bottom of the plaque. It costs around £4,200 to sponsor a plaque (once you’ve successfully passed the application).

It doesn’t have to be whole boroughs that organise a plaque scheme, sometimes it’s a tiny local community such as with the Marchmont Association centred around Marchmont Street in Bloomsbury.

[![Image 27](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ic_r!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9135a501-13ce-4576-88df-964bbb760f4f_1189x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ic_r!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9135a501-13ce-4576-88df-964bbb760f4f_1189x1080.png)

And often an institution might just focus on creating one single plaque in London, like the one commemorating Dr John Snow outside the pub named after him in Soho.

[![Image 28](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0XKP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2db6f948-eca9-4aef-8827-507e19433ef5_974x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0XKP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2db6f948-eca9-4aef-8827-507e19433ef5_974x1080.jpeg)

_Probably one of the only hexagonal plaques in London!_

# The Evolution of London's Blue Plaques

### How did they start? Why are they not all blue? Who decides who gets one? And what are the most unusual blue plaques in London?

[![Image 3: Look Up London (Katie)'s avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h2sb!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1b6b1be6-2414-49ef-ae8e-a9d8686737b3_700x700.jpeg)](https://substack.com/@lookuplondon)

One of the easiest ways to start learning about London’s history is to look out for blue plaques.

In this week’s post, I’m taking you through the history of the London’s blue (and other coloured!) plaques (the oldest and most extensive scheme in the world!)

Short and snappy, they’re a springboard for the curious to go and do more digging once their interest is piqued.

## The Evolution of Blue Plaques

Whenever I stop to think about it, blue plaques are truly amazing.

Although they began in London, now anyone who looks up all over the UK is treated to a clue about extraordinary contributions from former residents.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MD1n!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F69bcaa15-e6fb-4245-a32a-d94f4684a8da_2332x2505.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MD1n!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F69bcaa15-e6fb-4245-a32a-d94f4684a8da_2332x2505.jpeg)

_In front of Dame Millicent Fawcett’s blue plaque on a ‘Bloomsbury’s Inspiring Women’ walk!_

## But whose idea was it?

Along the stuccoed terraces of Belgravia, at 16 Eaton Place you can find a small blue plaque for William Ewart (1798-1869).

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wc3O!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F55e8f6de-4ca9-4692-9cdf-c0d980cb643c_768x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wc3O!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F55e8f6de-4ca9-4692-9cdf-c0d980cb643c_768x1024.jpeg)

_**[Blue Plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/william-ewart/)** at 16 Eaton Place, Belgravia – Image by **[Spudgun77](https://www.flickr.com/photos/24701549@N07/15699260348/)** CC BY 2.0_

A politician and reformer, what this plaque _doesn’t_ tell you is that the idea for blue plaques came from him!

I doubt that when William stood up in the House of Commons on 17 July 1863 anyone predicted the legacy **[his words](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/1863-07-17/debates/f5463ba6-1538-4b64-9ef7-cd1b3b641df5/CommonsChamber)** would have.

Might it be practical, William posed, _“to have inscribed on those houses in London which been inhabited by celebrated persons, the names of such persons.”_?

He continued to give possible examples of “_how rich the metropolis was in such associations”_ including John Milton at 19 York Street Westminster, Isaac Newton and Joshua Reynolds off Leicester Square and Dr Johnson in Gough Square.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9gBZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5be87f00-a4c3-4bfb-a39d-8a30ed49ae84_735x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9gBZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5be87f00-a4c3-4bfb-a39d-8a30ed49ae84_735x1024.jpeg)

_Action shot of me during a **[Fleet Street](https://lookup.london/walking-tours/fleet-street-walking-tour/)** walk in front of Dr Johnson’s plaque_

He concluded that _“other nations were in the habit of preserving memorial of their great men”_ and London should too.

What a great idea, right? But who could make it a reality…

## The Society of Arts

Someone who was paying attention was Sir Henry Cole, first Director of the Victoria and Albert Museum and the co-organiser of the Great Exhibition of 1851.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!F32b!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc286d98a-516d-413d-8055-3259204921d6_721x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!F32b!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc286d98a-516d-413d-8055-3259204921d6_721x1024.png)

_A mosaic featuring Henry Cole on the Ceramic Staircase in the V&A_

In July 1863 Cole wrote a letter to the journal of the Society of Arts (later the Royal Society of Arts or RSA) mentioning the parliamentary debate. He proposed that the RSA should take this scheme forward:

_“It seems to me a proper subject for the Society of Arts to consider. The object in view is of public interest, and refers especially to celebrities in arts, science, manufactures, commerce and literature.”_

Henry Cole’s blue plaque was **[erected](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/henry-cole/)** in 1991 opposite the V&A.

The Treasurer of the RSA was a man called George Bartley, someone keen to preserve London’s history and who already concerned that too much of the city’s heritage was being torn down in the early 1860s. He commissioned the Staffordshire potter, Herbert Minton to create two blue, circular ceramic plaques.

One was for the birthplace of Lord Byron on Holles Street and the other for Napoleon III who lived for a time on King Street.

These were erected in 1867 as London’s first blue plaques but now only one survives.

If you want to find London’s oldest blue plaque you just need to look up at 3 King Street in St James’s.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rYfg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8e71b571-7730-4222-ab34-e10c460fff99_992x991.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rYfg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8e71b571-7730-4222-ab34-e10c460fff99_992x991.jpeg)

The RSA managed the blue plaque scheme until 1901 but their plaques weren’t always blue, in fact the majority of the 35 erected were a terracotta brown.

You can easily identify the RSA plaques, not only by their matte finish but by the decorative edging that spells out ‘Erected by The Society of Arts’ interspaced with interlaced curved lines and little crosses.

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BZVA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedfed856-f7c5-4959-b67e-85ab35d1d3e9_979x979.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BZVA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fedfed856-f7c5-4959-b67e-85ab35d1d3e9_979x979.jpeg)

_John Dryden’s RSA plaque (that needs some tlc) on Gerrard Street in Chinatown_

A brown **[plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/dr-samuel-johnson/)** for Dr Samuel Johnson was erected in 1876 at 17 Gough Square, one of the people originally suggested by William Ewart back in 1863.

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!haQc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffedc07e2-7c53-4db1-961f-ca077cc4e894_1080x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!haQc!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffedc07e2-7c53-4db1-961f-ca077cc4e894_1080x1080.jpeg)

This plaque off Fleet Street is also unique because it’s the only _official_ blue plaque within the Square Mile.

## City of London Plaques

True to form, The City of London decided around 1879 that they would do things differently and manage their own scheme of plaques.

City of London plaques are still blue, but square and they tend to focus more on former buildings and institutions over individuals.

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NiIs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff8c1e0b4-ada5-43b2-80a9-c033f76b80a0_676x519.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NiIs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff8c1e0b4-ada5-43b2-80a9-c033f76b80a0_676x519.jpeg)

By my latest count there were 182 City of London plaques. Out of these only 38 commemorate actual people (with a _whopping_ 3 of those being women).

If you’re curious as to which three women are commemorated, they are Elizabeth Fry, **[Susanna Wesley](https://lookup.london/spital-yard-susanna-wesley/)** and Mary Harris Smith (the first woman to qualify as an accountant).

You can view an interactive map of the City of London Plaques **[here](https://www.mapping.cityoflondon.gov.uk/geocortex/mapping/?viewer=compass&runworkflowbyid=Switch_layer_themes&LayerTheme=Show%20the%20Heritage%20Estate%20layers)**.

From 1901 a new body took over the running of the blue plaque scheme…

## London County Council

The London County Council who were the local governing body for London from 1889 until 1965.

It was under them that the scheme really got going with hundreds of new plaques popping up across London.

[![Image 13](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xd-E!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5d71c076-b44a-4fbf-8d87-6a66cd88eafb_1080x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xd-E!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5d71c076-b44a-4fbf-8d87-6a66cd88eafb_1080x1080.jpeg)

_Thomas de Quincey’s Covent Garden plaque which spells his name wrong! It’s missing an ‘e’_

If you enjoy a bit of hard data, between 1903 and 1965 they erected 250 plaques and then under its new name (the Greater London Council) they put up a further 262.

At first the LCC have a similar design to the RSC plaques, with a decorative border and then the initials LCC at the top.

[![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fu8S!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6999e400-3902-4179-ad4e-437cc3c57525_1105x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fu8S!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6999e400-3902-4179-ad4e-437cc3c57525_1105x1080.png)

_3 Prime Ministers for the price of 1 in St James’s Square!_

They also experimented with a few different designs, one of the prettiest can still be found on Beak Street in Soho

[![Image 15](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AJ5Q!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F978be447-7b4a-4182-b821-b9822ecb3ee5_900x660.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AJ5Q!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F978be447-7b4a-4182-b821-b9822ecb3ee5_900x660.png)

_Love the succinct but charming wording on this **[plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/mary-hughes/)** at 71 Vallace Road, Whitechapel_

Over time the LCC and and then GLC blue plaques start to appear much more uniform.

They have the brighter blue colour and sheen as well as a more standardised format for the text. Typically it has the person’s name and their dates alongside a few words to describe them underneath.

[![Image 16](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Byr6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F81b2233a-53ac-41c7-8e78-a6c46b2025fa_923x924.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Byr6!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F81b2233a-53ac-41c7-8e78-a6c46b2025fa_923x924.jpeg)

_Love the succinct but charming wording on this **[plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/mary-hughes/)** at 71 Vallance Road, Whitechapel_

As blue plaques proliferated across the capital so did their prestige and power.

At 48 Doughty Street today you can find the **[Charles Dickens Museum](https://dickensmuseum.com/)**. In 1903 a LCC plaque was unveiled on the writer’s former home well before it became a museum (in 1925) and probably helped save the home from major renovation.

In the cases of blue plaques for Vincent Van Gogh, Oscar Wilde and D.H. Lawrence all helped to ensure that the homes were preserved for posterity rather than face demolition.

[![Image 17](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2LTP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8135c615-8d3e-4cd5-81df-fdc323fa0b18_1432x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2LTP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8135c615-8d3e-4cd5-81df-fdc323fa0b18_1432x1080.png)

_The LCC plaque – with beautiful decorative features – outside the Charles Dickens Museum_

One of my favourite plaques from the Greater London Council era is Edward Johnston’s plaque in Chiswick. Look properly and there’s something _off_ about it.

[![Image 18](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8mi6!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1afcbd26-3815-4c37-9442-6f5f9b51f40c_492x492.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8mi6!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1afcbd26-3815-4c37-9442-6f5f9b51f40c_492x492.jpeg)

It was Johnston that created the famous typeface still used by Transport For London today and this is the only plaque that uses that special font!

But another great one to spot arrives in 1986, when one of the final blue plaques they unveiled was to… themselves!

[![Image 19](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rE59!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1bab5c77-9871-4c62-88a3-2fb6cacdf62e_1062x862.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rE59!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1bab5c77-9871-4c62-88a3-2fb6cacdf62e_1062x862.jpeg)

An unusual design with an extra decorative border on **[County Hall](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/london-county-council/)**.

## English Heritage

Since 1986 the Blue Plaque Scheme has been managed by English Heritage, where often you can spot their logo at the bottom.

[![Image 20](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G-nT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F931711f9-c2d1-40e4-a708-34643c1e7b6a_1036x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G-nT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F931711f9-c2d1-40e4-a708-34643c1e7b6a_1036x1080.jpeg)

This charming [blue plaque](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/luke-howard/) is in Bruce Grove, Tottenham

Today all English Heritage blue plaques are still made by hand. For over 40 years they were made by Frank and Sue Ashworth but Sue sadly died in 2026. You can watch a lovely video of them working on the plaque for Freddie Mercury **[here](https://youtu.be/BAmnwsVfu1U?si=gSbVOcUi2tPsdBnx)**.

The immense task and privilege now falls to Ned Heywood and Julia Land from Ned Heywood Heritage Ceramics. Since 2018 they have been making ceramic plaques from their base in Chepstow.

In the decades that English Heritage have managed blue plaques, they’ve erected hundreds more plaques across London and now there are well over 1,000 total.

In recent years they’ve concentrated on honouring a more diverse selection of Londoners. In 2016 less than 4% of plaques represented Black or Asian people and only 15% of the total number of plaques were for women and you can read more about their plans on the English Heritage website **here**.

[![Image 21](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!B8dD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F588a336c-bade-49e8-9cff-f771598ef776_861x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!B8dD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F588a336c-bade-49e8-9cff-f771598ef776_861x1080.jpeg)

## Who Gets a Blue Plaque?

Anyone can nominate a person to receive an English Heritage blue plaque.

[![Image 23](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Nuyj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb3775e54-9bac-4781-bd91-55ea78d856a9_1024x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Nuyj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb3775e54-9bac-4781-bd91-55ea78d856a9_1024x1024.png)

_The LCC plaque for John Howard on Great Ormond Street in Bloomsbury_

These proposals are considered by a panel, but the general rules are that 1) the person has to have been dead for 20 years and 2) they have made a ‘positive contribution to human welfare and happiness’.

It’s also important that the person commemorated has a longstanding association with the building (they didn’t just stay overnight one time!) and it helps if the building is the original.

You can read more about submitting a blue plaque request **[here](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/propose-a-plaque/)**.

## Green and other ‘Unofficial’ Plaques

It’s not just the City of London that wanted to celebrate local history via their own scheme.

Many other London boroughs or independent societies have their own versions and English Heritage **[lists](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/siteassets/home/visit/blue-plaques/propose-plaque/other-plaque-schemes.pdf)** 32 different schemes from which here are just a few examples of the variety you can find across London.

[![Image 24](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9J5-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89c8d101-7495-48ad-8686-06650a6e15b1_625x651.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9J5-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89c8d101-7495-48ad-8686-06650a6e15b1_625x651.jpeg)

_One of the Islington Council People’s Plaques (Est. 2010)_

[![Image 25](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IF8m!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3eff0c57-0d73-4344-beeb-990c86102248_768x1024.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IF8m!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3eff0c57-0d73-4344-beeb-990c86102248_768x1024.jpeg)

_A Bow Heritage Trail plaque, unveiled in the 1990s_

The City of Westminster launched their own scheme in 1991 with the criteria of being eminent, deserving of recognition and reasonably well known. Like English Heritage there also has to have been a sufficient amount of time since their death to ensure their lasting legacy.

[![Image 26](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V4xy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75adfb04-2d8d-4f64-87a6-a0a7fa38ae4e_1024x952.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V4xy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75adfb04-2d8d-4f64-87a6-a0a7fa38ae4e_1024x952.png)

_Jeremy Bentham’s plaque on Queen Anne’s Gate, Westminster_

Many of the Westminster plaques are sponsored, the main sponsor being named at the bottom of the plaque. It costs around £4,200 to sponsor a plaque (once you’ve successfully passed the application).

It doesn’t have to be whole boroughs that organise a plaque scheme, sometimes it’s a tiny local community such as with the Marchmont Association centred around Marchmont Street in Bloomsbury.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a list of the 1018 [blue plaques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_plaques "Blue plaques") placed by [English Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Heritage "English Heritage") and its predecessors in the [boroughs of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_boroughs "London boroughs"), the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster"), and the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London"). The scheme includes a small number of plaques that were erected privately and subsequently absorbed.

The scheme began in 1866.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_English_Heritage_blue_plaques_in_London#cite_note-1) It was originally administered by the [Royal Society of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_Arts "Royal Society of Arts") until 1901 when it was taken over the [London County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_County_Council "London County Council"). The LCC ran the scheme until its abolition in 1965 when its successor body the [Greater London Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Council "Greater London Council") (GLC) took charge. Since the abolition of the GLC in 1986, the blue plaque scheme has been administered by [English Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Heritage "English Heritage").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a list of the 1018 [blue plaques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_plaques "Blue plaques") placed by [English Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Heritage "English Heritage") and its predecessors in the [boroughs of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_boroughs "London boroughs"), the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster"), and the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London"). The scheme includes a small number of plaques that were erected privately and subsequently absorbed.

The scheme began in 1866.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_English_Heritage_blue_plaques_in_London#cite_note-1) It was originally administered by the [Royal Society of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_Arts "Royal Society of Arts") until 1901 when it was taken over the [London County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_County_Council "London County Council"). The LCC ran the scheme until its abolition in 1965 when its successor body the [Greater London Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Council "Greater London Council") (GLC) took charge. Since the abolition of the GLC in 1986, the blue plaque scheme has been administered by [English Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Heritage "English Heritage").

# Blue Plaques of London. Who are these people? No, I mean really, who are they?

![Image 3](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464802993225-CV1LK6JVFSFYU3004QQD/image-asset.jpeg)

I run entirely on caffeine and sarcasm. In that order. So as I have been strolling the streets of London with a venti latte in hand I have been seeing these blue medallions or plaques all over the city with names and sometimes professions that I have never heard of.For those of you that don’t know what a [**Blue Plaque**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_plaque) is let me give you a very brief description. Blue Plaques (not always blue but mostly) are given out by the**London Heritage Society**to recognize people of importance (not always British) who have lived, died or done something big in London. It usually marks a home, place of business or site where this notable event occurred. They are everywhere around London and currently there are over [**900**](http://reeddesign.co.uk/inspiration/blueplaques/)Blue Plaques adhered to the walls of buildings commemorating that special person who spent time there. They are kinda a big deal. There is even one across the street from me, writer James Joyce (him I know) which I guess is what started my curiosity for these plaques.

![Image 4: Tom Cribb, Bare Knuckle Fighter](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464803796803-LU7KP1PI3VZ4O5VXSZO6/image-asset.jpeg)

_Tom Cribb, Bare Knuckle Fighter_

So how is it that of over 900 names I have absolutely no idea who most of them are?That is not to say just because I don’t know who they are doesn’t mean they are not worthy of such a distinction. Maybe it is I who needs to brush up on my British history. But I think most Londoners don’t’ know these names either unless of course they are either massively noteworthy i.e.)Winston Churchill or Mozart or are directly tied into a local Quiz Night question and answer, then at the very least my English cousins absolutely would know who they are. I think the reason most people don’t recognize these Blue Plaque names (assuming that they don’t) is that a lot of them lived a very long time ago plus some,as I have discovered truly are very obscure. Lets start with[**Luke Howard 1772-1864 “Namer Of Clouds**](https://www.rmets.org/weather-and-climate/observing/luke-howard-and-cloud-names)”. What an interesting profession (caffeine is in full effect and now the sarcasm).I could and would happily name clouds and proudly accept a Blue Plaque for doing so. I even know what I would name my first cloud, “Bam Bam”, a name quite suited for a cloud I think. Named after my first family cat (not Barney Rubble’s son, although that technically is who the cat was named after).

![Image 5: Joseph Grimaldi, Clown (really!)](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1465077870241-ZEAWSN809G3F08HUYN1P/image-asset.jpeg)

_Joseph Grimaldi, Clown (really!)_

Who could deny the contribution of one [**Joseph Grimaldi**](http://www.vam.ac.uk/content/articles/g/grimaldi-the-clown/), Clown. Check out his picture. Maybe he was the first creepy clown to start scaring children?Or Queen Victoria's dentist Sir Edwin Saunders. I am guessing that back in Queen Victoria's day it was dentists like Sir Edwin that helped give Britain the reputation they still have to this day for perfect teeth.Another “interesting” one is [**Tom Cribb**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cribb), “Bare Knuckle Fighter”. I can only guess that in the time of Mr Cribb's dedication (early 1800’s) there might have been a serious shortage of candidates who fought with covered knuckles.

But in amongst the obscure and ancient there are some that I not only know, but adore. People who made a little dent or impression on me personally. So I went in search of my own "Blue Plaque Walk of Fame" looking for those that made a difference... to me.

![Image 6: Freddie Mercury on tour with Queen. 1986](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464803931543-2884TM0KY0O063V7TYIS/image-asset.jpeg)

_Freddie Mercury on tour with Queen. 1986_

![Image 7](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784589344-99NAUNGD7GSFU8N5ZKTJ/image-asset.jpeg)

The first on my list is one of the newest inductees this year, Queen’s lead singer [**Freddie Mercury**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury). He just got his plaque almost 25 years after his death. Can you believe it has almost been 25 years?The London Heritage Society has a 20 year rule before they will consider giving a Blue Plaque. They want to make sure that the person is still relevant years later, just like Joseph Grimaldi, Clown.I first saw Queen back in high school with Dave Bradshaw on my very first concert-date (where are you now Dave Bradshaw?) That was a few summers ago. Even now a generation later you would be hard pressed to find someone who can’t shake his or her head in perfect timing to Bohemian Rhapsody a-la Wayne’s World or sing We Are The Champions at some sporting event.The plaque was put on his childhood home in Feltham, west London where he first lived as Farrokh Bulsara when he and his family immigrated to England from Zanzibar.

But what I found puzzling is that they didn’t put the [**Blue Plaque**](http://www.nme.com/news/freddie-mercury/91867)on his home in Kensington, the house where he lived and died in as “Freddy Mercury”. It was rumoured that when he knew he was dying Mercury and band mate Brian May wrote the song “The Show Must Go On” in this house, foreshadowing Freddie’s impending death. There was even a question if Freddie would have been even able to sing this song as he was very sick at the time.But Freddie was quoted as saying, “I'll fucking do it darling, vodka down”. And did it he did, he lacerated that vocal. Clearly Brian May really meant the show must go on as he is currently touring Queen again with American Idol finalist Adam Lambert taking on lead vocals. Great vocalist Adam but sorry Brian May, Queen is not Queen without Freddie Mercury.

![Image 8: Signing the wall at 1 Logan Place, Kensington. Former home of Freddie Mercury.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784473760-9OZ5CZB9R7RZFO616WAL/Fan+leaves+message+at+former+home+of+Freddie+Mercury)

_Signing the wall at 1 Logan Place, Kensington. Former home of Freddie Mercury._

So I visited Mercury's house in Kensington and now almost 25 years after Freddy died people are still there, leaving hand-written notes, writing on the brick wall that surrounds the mansion with lipstick (or a Sharpie), leaving flowers at the very unassuming gate surrounded by an 14 foot wall, marked with graffiti by a thousand different fans. When I came to check it out there was a small group of people there signing the wall, taking pictures. One woman wiped a tear from her eye, looked at me and smiled. Almost 25 years later the shrine created by his fans still lives on! I walked away very touched thinking that no one should never, EVER underestimate the power of music.

![Image 9: Handwritten messages attached to the wall outside Mercury's former house.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784342381-40J2AXPMESB5G4WIKFPS/Messages+to+Freddie+Mercury)

_Handwritten messages attached to the wall outside Mercury's former house._

![Image 10: Former Freddie Mercury house with no mention of him ever living there.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784703473-E1GH9VROU7ZXYINIKGPE/image-asset.jpeg)

_Former Freddie Mercury house with no mention of him ever living there._

Only a few blocks from this house was another house that Mercury use to live in. What I also found odd that not only was there no mentioned of Freddie at this house but rather there was a plaque for someone else. A one Mr. Edward Linley Sambourne, a cartoonist who lived there between 1844-1910. I am certain that if Mr. Sambourne had he been living he would have happily and proudly shared some wall space with Freddie Mercury.

Next on my tour was the infamous horror and suspense film director,[**Alfred Hitchcock**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock). He was on a very busy street not far from Freddie but truly a world away. What was so fantastic about Hitchcock’s house was it looked like something out of one of his horror films. It looked like if [**Norman Bates**](http://www.imdb.com/character/ch0003067/bio)had a flat in London this is where he would be living. It was dark, rundown and gave me the creeps. How totally prefect.

![Image 11: Alfred Hitchcock's former creepy house in Kensington, London.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464785161285-RZKDVQ8FK2UM6MU27UYR/Former+home+of+Alfred+Hitchcock)

_Alfred Hitchcock's former creepy house in Kensington, London._

![Image 12](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464868242539-H7Z5O37GN109XTDFY3YY/image-asset.jpeg)

![Image 13: Former house of Oscar Wilde, Chelsea.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464813285234-3Q88VNXYJAPCA6I80O8A/Former+Home+of+Oscar+Wilde)

_Former house of Oscar Wilde, Chelsea_.

I then went off in search of[**Oscar Wilde**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Wilde) in Chelsea. He lived in a much finer neighbourhood and street than Alfred. I have to say that I love everything about Oscar Wilde. There were a few other unknown plaques on his street but honestly it was too much effort to find a place to rest my latte to take a photo as I was there to see Oscar. Interesting that his plaque did not say "writer" but rather, "wit and dramatist". I am guessing Wilde for sure knew a little something about drama in his life but not to say he was a writer? Seriously? How did that happen? On a similar theme American actress Ava Gardner recently got her Blue Plaque. Her plaque doesn't refer to her as an "actress"even though she acted in over 60 films, but rather a "Movie Star". I guess unless you are quoting Shakespeare the Heritage Society doesn't consider it acting.

I quote Oscar Wilde more often than I do any other "wit and dramatist"with the single possible exception of Dr. Seuss who sadly could not be part of this tour. My favourite quote of Wilde’s and it likely summed up how he lived his life is, “once is curiosity twice perversion”. So true, especially if you have ever been to Vegas. When I was in Paris a few years ago I visited his grave in the [**Père Lachaise Cemetery**](http://www.perelachaisecemetery.com/). His tombstone was a large Egyptian-like sculpture and it is now protected by a giant enclosure of plexi-glass. On the plexi people would kiss it deliberately leaving their lipstick marks. I was not able to find out what the significance of the lipstick on the tomb of a gay man was but if you ever get a chance you must visit this cemetery, it was fascinating. The Doors frontman Jim Morrison is also buried there. His gravesite is littered with empty Jack Daniel's bottles. That I get.

![Image 14: Oscar Wilde's tombstone at Père Lachaise Cemetery](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464805229977-PG9NXXTPRDG0NNGW4VBF/Oscar+Wilde%27s+tomb+at+P%C3%A8re+Lachaise+Cemetery%2C+Paris)

_Oscar Wilde's tombstone at Père Lachaise Cemetery_

![Image 15](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464785492692-41P2FW46DNENOHK77ZUF/image-asset.jpeg)

I then went off to Marylebone in search of [**John Lennon**.](http://www.biography.com/people/john-lennon-9379045) I had my ear-buds in and “Imagine” was the soundtrack that accompanied me. This tour really is enhanced with music. Randomly a song by Julian Lennon (John’ son) called “Lucy” came on that I didn’t even know I had in my music library. It played as I was standing outside of Lennon’s house. How serendipitous. It is crazy how much Julian sounds like his dad and I wondered if the chorus “we still love you Lucy” had anything to do with Lucy in The Sky With Diamonds? The house was a typical but lovely English row house, well kept and somehow I think the plaque saying John Lennon lived there immediately increased the property value.

Lucy

Julian Lennon & James Scott Cook

0:00

_Have a listen._

![Image 16: John Lennon's house in Marylebone, London](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1465086038620-PRVLQ0M4WI0FARRI5J36/Former+home+of+John+Lennon%2C+London)

_John Lennon's house in Marylebone, London_

I then walked to Mayfair to see the two neighbours who lived next door to each other hundreds of years apart. Composer [**George Frideric Handel**](http://www.biography.com/people/george-handel-9327378)of 25 Brook St and at number 23 and a totally different type of musician to Handel, rocker and member of the [**27 Club**](http://www.biography.com/people/groups/the-27-club)[**Jimi Hendrix.**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix)It certainly took away some the “edge” that I associate with Hendrix that his house was in Mayfair, a very posh upper-crust neighbourhood. You would have thought based on his persona and clearly how he lived (and died) he would have been in a neighbourhood that was artsy and have a lot more edge, like Shoreditch.Not in the heart of the most expensive shops and exclusive hotels in London.There is now a Jo Malone store on the street level of his former house. He would have not approved but I am guessing it smells much better now than it did when he lived there.

![Image 17: 23 and 25 Brook St, Mayfair. Former residences of Hendrix and Handel.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464805508937-S3COQ6WOJZJZWFRVQQZS/Former+homes+of+Jimi+Hendrix+and+Handel)

_23 and 25 Brook St, Mayfair. Former residences of Hendrix and Handel._

![Image 18: Former home of Ian Fleming. How cool if instead of the Mercedes parked out front there was an Aston Martin (or cooler the flying car from Chitty Chitty Bang Bang).](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464805695575-BWDOYYQMD0MJJ4A9LLC9/image-asset.jpeg)

_Former home of Ian Fleming. How cool if instead of the Mercedes parked out front there was an Aston Martin (or cooler the flying car from Chitty Chitty Bang Bang)._

Finally, and this visit was mostly inspired by Bruce and my dad, I went to Belgravia to visit the home of [**Ian Fleming**](http://www.biography.com/people/ian-fleming-9296920), creator of James Bond.More personally significant to me was that Ian Fleming also wrote "Chitty Chitty Bang Bang" (clearly I am not a Bond girl). I loved Chitty Chitty Bang Bang and was very afraid of the evil villain the Kid-Catcher as a child. He still is in my opinion one of the greatest villains of all time. Fleming lived on a very nice street in a very wealthy neighbourhood and he too had a few Blue Plaque neighbours that I have never heard of. The London Heritage Society has come under fire lately for being a prominently white, male panel that allegedly tends to favour white, male honourees. Does this not sound just like the Oscars?I think [**Jada and Will Smith**](http://www.dailymail.co.uk/tvshowbiz/article-3405235/It-responsibility-make-change-Jada-Pinkett-Smith-reveals-s-boycotting-Oscars-series-Tweets-questioning-lack-nominations-people-color.html) would happily fight against this injustice too if they had even the slightness thing to gain from this.

![Image 19: Message at the home of Freddie Mercury](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1465234960629-KWE9A0714VRD5S3Y83HG/Message+at+the+home+of+Freddie+Mercury)

I will continue to explore and learn about these Blue Plaque people who I am certain at some point, in some real way contributed to the world of London even if was to name clouds. There is still Vincent Van Gogh, Mozart, Charles Dickens, Keith Moon, Charlie Chaplin or Noel Coward (for my mom) that are on my list to find,see and take a moment to remember.For in the words of the incredible and very quotable Dr Suess, “oh the things you can find, if you don’t stay behind”.

# Blue Plaques of London. Who are these people? No, I mean really, who are they?

![Image 3](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464802993225-CV1LK6JVFSFYU3004QQD/image-asset.jpeg)

I run entirely on caffeine and sarcasm. In that order. So as I have been strolling the streets of London with a venti latte in hand I have been seeing these blue medallions or plaques all over the city with names and sometimes professions that I have never heard of.For those of you that don’t know what a [**Blue Plaque**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_plaque) is let me give you a very brief description. Blue Plaques (not always blue but mostly) are given out by the**London Heritage Society**to recognize people of importance (not always British) who have lived, died or done something big in London. It usually marks a home, place of business or site where this notable event occurred. They are everywhere around London and currently there are over [**900**](http://reeddesign.co.uk/inspiration/blueplaques/)Blue Plaques adhered to the walls of buildings commemorating that special person who spent time there. They are kinda a big deal. There is even one across the street from me, writer James Joyce (him I know) which I guess is what started my curiosity for these plaques.

![Image 4: Tom Cribb, Bare Knuckle Fighter](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464803796803-LU7KP1PI3VZ4O5VXSZO6/image-asset.jpeg)

_Tom Cribb, Bare Knuckle Fighter_

So how is it that of over 900 names I have absolutely no idea who most of them are?That is not to say just because I don’t know who they are doesn’t mean they are not worthy of such a distinction. Maybe it is I who needs to brush up on my British history. But I think most Londoners don’t’ know these names either unless of course they are either massively noteworthy i.e.)Winston Churchill or Mozart or are directly tied into a local Quiz Night question and answer, then at the very least my English cousins absolutely would know who they are. I think the reason most people don’t recognize these Blue Plaque names (assuming that they don’t) is that a lot of them lived a very long time ago plus some,as I have discovered truly are very obscure. Lets start with[**Luke Howard 1772-1864 “Namer Of Clouds**](https://www.rmets.org/weather-and-climate/observing/luke-howard-and-cloud-names)”. What an interesting profession (caffeine is in full effect and now the sarcasm).I could and would happily name clouds and proudly accept a Blue Plaque for doing so. I even know what I would name my first cloud, “Bam Bam”, a name quite suited for a cloud I think. Named after my first family cat (not Barney Rubble’s son, although that technically is who the cat was named after).

![Image 5: Joseph Grimaldi, Clown (really!)](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1465077870241-ZEAWSN809G3F08HUYN1P/image-asset.jpeg)

_Joseph Grimaldi, Clown (really!)_

Who could deny the contribution of one [**Joseph Grimaldi**](http://www.vam.ac.uk/content/articles/g/grimaldi-the-clown/), Clown. Check out his picture. Maybe he was the first creepy clown to start scaring children?Or Queen Victoria's dentist Sir Edwin Saunders. I am guessing that back in Queen Victoria's day it was dentists like Sir Edwin that helped give Britain the reputation they still have to this day for perfect teeth.Another “interesting” one is [**Tom Cribb**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cribb), “Bare Knuckle Fighter”. I can only guess that in the time of Mr Cribb's dedication (early 1800’s) there might have been a serious shortage of candidates who fought with covered knuckles.

But in amongst the obscure and ancient there are some that I not only know, but adore. People who made a little dent or impression on me personally. So I went in search of my own "Blue Plaque Walk of Fame" looking for those that made a difference... to me.

![Image 6: Freddie Mercury on tour with Queen. 1986](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464803931543-2884TM0KY0O063V7TYIS/image-asset.jpeg)

_Freddie Mercury on tour with Queen. 1986_

![Image 7](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784589344-99NAUNGD7GSFU8N5ZKTJ/image-asset.jpeg)

The first on my list is one of the newest inductees this year, Queen’s lead singer [**Freddie Mercury**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury). He just got his plaque almost 25 years after his death. Can you believe it has almost been 25 years?The London Heritage Society has a 20 year rule before they will consider giving a Blue Plaque. They want to make sure that the person is still relevant years later, just like Joseph Grimaldi, Clown.I first saw Queen back in high school with Dave Bradshaw on my very first concert-date (where are you now Dave Bradshaw?) That was a few summers ago. Even now a generation later you would be hard pressed to find someone who can’t shake his or her head in perfect timing to Bohemian Rhapsody a-la Wayne’s World or sing We Are The Champions at some sporting event.The plaque was put on his childhood home in Feltham, west London where he first lived as Farrokh Bulsara when he and his family immigrated to England from Zanzibar.

But what I found puzzling is that they didn’t put the [**Blue Plaque**](http://www.nme.com/news/freddie-mercury/91867)on his home in Kensington, the house where he lived and died in as “Freddy Mercury”. It was rumoured that when he knew he was dying Mercury and band mate Brian May wrote the song “The Show Must Go On” in this house, foreshadowing Freddie’s impending death. There was even a question if Freddie would have been even able to sing this song as he was very sick at the time.But Freddie was quoted as saying, “I'll fucking do it darling, vodka down”. And did it he did, he lacerated that vocal. Clearly Brian May really meant the show must go on as he is currently touring Queen again with American Idol finalist Adam Lambert taking on lead vocals. Great vocalist Adam but sorry Brian May, Queen is not Queen without Freddie Mercury.

![Image 8: Signing the wall at 1 Logan Place, Kensington. Former home of Freddie Mercury.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784473760-9OZ5CZB9R7RZFO616WAL/Fan+leaves+message+at+former+home+of+Freddie+Mercury)

_Signing the wall at 1 Logan Place, Kensington. Former home of Freddie Mercury._

So I visited Mercury's house in Kensington and now almost 25 years after Freddy died people are still there, leaving hand-written notes, writing on the brick wall that surrounds the mansion with lipstick (or a Sharpie), leaving flowers at the very unassuming gate surrounded by an 14 foot wall, marked with graffiti by a thousand different fans. When I came to check it out there was a small group of people there signing the wall, taking pictures. One woman wiped a tear from her eye, looked at me and smiled. Almost 25 years later the shrine created by his fans still lives on! I walked away very touched thinking that no one should never, EVER underestimate the power of music.

![Image 9: Handwritten messages attached to the wall outside Mercury's former house.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784342381-40J2AXPMESB5G4WIKFPS/Messages+to+Freddie+Mercury)

_Handwritten messages attached to the wall outside Mercury's former house._

![Image 10: Former Freddie Mercury house with no mention of him ever living there.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464784703473-E1GH9VROU7ZXYINIKGPE/image-asset.jpeg)

_Former Freddie Mercury house with no mention of him ever living there._

Only a few blocks from this house was another house that Mercury use to live in. What I also found odd that not only was there no mentioned of Freddie at this house but rather there was a plaque for someone else. A one Mr. Edward Linley Sambourne, a cartoonist who lived there between 1844-1910. I am certain that if Mr. Sambourne had he been living he would have happily and proudly shared some wall space with Freddie Mercury.

Next on my tour was the infamous horror and suspense film director,[**Alfred Hitchcock**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock). He was on a very busy street not far from Freddie but truly a world away. What was so fantastic about Hitchcock’s house was it looked like something out of one of his horror films. It looked like if [**Norman Bates**](http://www.imdb.com/character/ch0003067/bio)had a flat in London this is where he would be living. It was dark, rundown and gave me the creeps. How totally prefect.

![Image 11: Alfred Hitchcock's former creepy house in Kensington, London.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464785161285-RZKDVQ8FK2UM6MU27UYR/Former+home+of+Alfred+Hitchcock)

_Alfred Hitchcock's former creepy house in Kensington, London._

![Image 12](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464868242539-H7Z5O37GN109XTDFY3YY/image-asset.jpeg)

![Image 13: Former house of Oscar Wilde, Chelsea.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464813285234-3Q88VNXYJAPCA6I80O8A/Former+Home+of+Oscar+Wilde)

_Former house of Oscar Wilde, Chelsea_.

I then went off in search of[**Oscar Wilde**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Wilde) in Chelsea. He lived in a much finer neighbourhood and street than Alfred. I have to say that I love everything about Oscar Wilde. There were a few other unknown plaques on his street but honestly it was too much effort to find a place to rest my latte to take a photo as I was there to see Oscar. Interesting that his plaque did not say "writer" but rather, "wit and dramatist". I am guessing Wilde for sure knew a little something about drama in his life but not to say he was a writer? Seriously? How did that happen? On a similar theme American actress Ava Gardner recently got her Blue Plaque. Her plaque doesn't refer to her as an "actress"even though she acted in over 60 films, but rather a "Movie Star". I guess unless you are quoting Shakespeare the Heritage Society doesn't consider it acting.

I quote Oscar Wilde more often than I do any other "wit and dramatist"with the single possible exception of Dr. Seuss who sadly could not be part of this tour. My favourite quote of Wilde’s and it likely summed up how he lived his life is, “once is curiosity twice perversion”. So true, especially if you have ever been to Vegas. When I was in Paris a few years ago I visited his grave in the [**Père Lachaise Cemetery**](http://www.perelachaisecemetery.com/). His tombstone was a large Egyptian-like sculpture and it is now protected by a giant enclosure of plexi-glass. On the plexi people would kiss it deliberately leaving their lipstick marks. I was not able to find out what the significance of the lipstick on the tomb of a gay man was but if you ever get a chance you must visit this cemetery, it was fascinating. The Doors frontman Jim Morrison is also buried there. His gravesite is littered with empty Jack Daniel's bottles. That I get.

![Image 14: Oscar Wilde's tombstone at Père Lachaise Cemetery](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464805229977-PG9NXXTPRDG0NNGW4VBF/Oscar+Wilde%27s+tomb+at+P%C3%A8re+Lachaise+Cemetery%2C+Paris)

_Oscar Wilde's tombstone at Père Lachaise Cemetery_

![Image 15](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464785492692-41P2FW46DNENOHK77ZUF/image-asset.jpeg)

I then went off to Marylebone in search of [**John Lennon**.](http://www.biography.com/people/john-lennon-9379045) I had my ear-buds in and “Imagine” was the soundtrack that accompanied me. This tour really is enhanced with music. Randomly a song by Julian Lennon (John’ son) called “Lucy” came on that I didn’t even know I had in my music library. It played as I was standing outside of Lennon’s house. How serendipitous. It is crazy how much Julian sounds like his dad and I wondered if the chorus “we still love you Lucy” had anything to do with Lucy in The Sky With Diamonds? The house was a typical but lovely English row house, well kept and somehow I think the plaque saying John Lennon lived there immediately increased the property value.

Lucy

Julian Lennon & James Scott Cook

0:00

_Have a listen._

![Image 16: John Lennon's house in Marylebone, London](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1465086038620-PRVLQ0M4WI0FARRI5J36/Former+home+of+John+Lennon%2C+London)

_John Lennon's house in Marylebone, London_

I then walked to Mayfair to see the two neighbours who lived next door to each other hundreds of years apart. Composer [**George Frideric Handel**](http://www.biography.com/people/george-handel-9327378)of 25 Brook St and at number 23 and a totally different type of musician to Handel, rocker and member of the [**27 Club**](http://www.biography.com/people/groups/the-27-club)[**Jimi Hendrix.**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix)It certainly took away some the “edge” that I associate with Hendrix that his house was in Mayfair, a very posh upper-crust neighbourhood. You would have thought based on his persona and clearly how he lived (and died) he would have been in a neighbourhood that was artsy and have a lot more edge, like Shoreditch.Not in the heart of the most expensive shops and exclusive hotels in London.There is now a Jo Malone store on the street level of his former house. He would have not approved but I am guessing it smells much better now than it did when he lived there.

![Image 17: 23 and 25 Brook St, Mayfair. Former residences of Hendrix and Handel.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464805508937-S3COQ6WOJZJZWFRVQQZS/Former+homes+of+Jimi+Hendrix+and+Handel)

_23 and 25 Brook St, Mayfair. Former residences of Hendrix and Handel._

![Image 18: Former home of Ian Fleming. How cool if instead of the Mercedes parked out front there was an Aston Martin (or cooler the flying car from Chitty Chitty Bang Bang).](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1464805695575-BWDOYYQMD0MJJ4A9LLC9/image-asset.jpeg)

_Former home of Ian Fleming. How cool if instead of the Mercedes parked out front there was an Aston Martin (or cooler the flying car from Chitty Chitty Bang Bang)._

Finally, and this visit was mostly inspired by Bruce and my dad, I went to Belgravia to visit the home of [**Ian Fleming**](http://www.biography.com/people/ian-fleming-9296920), creator of James Bond.More personally significant to me was that Ian Fleming also wrote "Chitty Chitty Bang Bang" (clearly I am not a Bond girl). I loved Chitty Chitty Bang Bang and was very afraid of the evil villain the Kid-Catcher as a child. He still is in my opinion one of the greatest villains of all time. Fleming lived on a very nice street in a very wealthy neighbourhood and he too had a few Blue Plaque neighbours that I have never heard of. The London Heritage Society has come under fire lately for being a prominently white, male panel that allegedly tends to favour white, male honourees. Does this not sound just like the Oscars?I think [**Jada and Will Smith**](http://www.dailymail.co.uk/tvshowbiz/article-3405235/It-responsibility-make-change-Jada-Pinkett-Smith-reveals-s-boycotting-Oscars-series-Tweets-questioning-lack-nominations-people-color.html) would happily fight against this injustice too if they had even the slightness thing to gain from this.

![Image 19: Message at the home of Freddie Mercury](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/571b75339f7266bb8a3dd3df/1465234960629-KWE9A0714VRD5S3Y83HG/Message+at+the+home+of+Freddie+Mercury)

I will continue to explore and learn about these Blue Plaque people who I am certain at some point, in some real way contributed to the world of London even if was to name clouds. There is still Vincent Van Gogh, Mozart, Charles Dickens, Keith Moon, Charlie Chaplin or Noel Coward (for my mom) that are on my list to find,see and take a moment to remember.For in the words of the incredible and very quotable Dr Suess, “oh the things you can find, if you don’t stay behind”.
